alt-001.zusammenfassung: The French city of Grenoble has proven that commercial outdoor advertising is not without alternatives. Instead of renewing advertising contracts, commercial surfaces were dismantled or replaced with citizen information and art.
alt-001.kernbefund: In 2014, the mayor of Grenoble decided to remove 326 commercial advertising billboards from public space. Instead of the expected commercial vacuum, 50 new surfaces were created for local cultural and social announcements. The city planted trees at the former advertising sites. The loss in advertising revenue (approx. 600,000 euros) was offset by cuts to the mayor's representation budget and by the positive effects of the improved quality of life.
alt-001.relevanz: This example refutes the industry's argument that cities are financially dependent on outdoor advertising. Public space can be actively used for cultural promotion, art, and greening, rather than being privatized for advertising corporations.

alt-002.zusammenfassung: The argument that outdoor advertising is necessary to fund bus and tram stops is structurally flawed. There are more sustainable, advertising-free financing models.
alt-002.kernbefund: Cities frequently exchange the provision of bus shelters for extensive advertising rights (Public-Private Partnerships). However, analyses show that the indirect costs — electricity consumption of the displays, traffic distraction, induced CO2 emissions — often outweigh the apparent financial benefit. Alternatively, cities like São Paulo (following the advertising ban "Cidade Limpa") finance their infrastructure through redistributed levies, taxes on vacant properties, or municipal self-financing, thereby retaining full control over the design and energy consumption of their street furniture.
alt-002.relevanz: Infrastructure financing is often used as a tool of leverage by the AdTech industry. Decoupling street furniture from advertising exploitation is fiscally feasible and leads to better, advertising-free urban spaces.

alt-003.zusammenfassung: The infrastructure of outdoor advertising can be repurposed subversively. A project in Tehran demonstrated the enormous social and psychological healing effect of art in place of consumer pressure.
alt-003.kernbefund: In May 2015, the mayor of Tehran (Iran) ordered that all approximately 1,500 commercial advertising billboards in the metropolis be pasted over for ten days as part of the project "A Gallery as Big as a Town." Instead of advertisements for smartphones and detergents, the billboards suddenly displayed works by Picasso, Matisse, Munch, and traditional Persian art. The experiment demonstrated impressively that the logistical infrastructure of the advertising industry can be used to transform a city into a giant open-air gallery and provide citizens with genuine cultural added value.
alt-003.relevanz: The project visualised the "what if": a world in which billboards do not belong to the highest bidder, but instead serve the public and cultural interests of urban society.

alt-004.zusammenfassung: Some Scandinavian cities demonstrate that modern urban development ("Smart City") is more successful without the visual and psychological burden of outdoor advertising.
alt-004.kernbefund: In various urban development projects across Scandinavia (e.g. in districts of Oslo or Stockholm), a "Human-Centric" approach is pursued that prioritises the reduction of visual noise. When planning connected infrastructure (smart lamp posts, information kiosks), the integration of advertising displays is deliberately avoided. Instead, these surfaces are used for real-time citizen information, climate data, or simple greenery. Studies show that citizens in these advertising-free spaces experience a greater sense of security, less stress, and stronger social cohesion, which increases the long-term attractiveness of the location.
alt-004.relevanz: The example proves that "Smart City" does not automatically have to mean "advertising city." A technologically advanced city can consciously choose visual tranquillity in order to place the well-being of its residents at the centre of its development.

culture-001.zusammenfassung: Academic analysis of advertising as a culturally homogenising force in the ASEAN region. Examines how international advertising challenges national cultural projects and spreads Western cultural elements worldwide.
culture-001.kernbefund: International advertising — particularly for global brands in public space — functions as a global cultural homogenisation force. It spreads a unified Western (primarily American) visual identity and value system across national borders, displacing local cultural ideals.
culture-001.relevanz: Outdoor advertising by McDonald's, Coca-Cola, Apple, and other global brands in public space shapes the visual identity of cities worldwide in an almost identical manner — at the expense of local cultural distinctiveness.

culture-002.zusammenfassung: Academic analysis of how global advertising and consumer culture contribute to the emergence of a homogeneous global culture. Specifically examines global brands (Coca-Cola, Apple, McDonald's) and their effect on cultural convergence.
culture-002.kernbefund: Global brands impose a consistent image and value system across national borders, promoting cultural convergence. Local cultural ideals — including beauty standards — are increasingly aligning with Western norms. Outdoor advertising is the primary channel through which these messages penetrate public space.
culture-002.relevanz: Every billboard for a Western global product in public space is an act of cultural overwriting (Überformung) — it sets Western standards as the norm without local communities being able to vote on it.

culture-003.zusammenfassung: Current (2024) analysis of how global advertising platforms and media — including outdoor advertising — contribute to cultural homogenisation and threaten local traditions and diversity.
culture-003.kernbefund: Global advertising and media platforms contribute measurably to cultural homogenisation. Local traditions and cultural diversity are being displaced by the dominance of global brand messages in public space. This is a currently growing problem.
culture-003.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is physically anchored in public space and is therefore a particularly persistent part of the cultural environment. Digital DOOH (Digital Out-of-Home) screens accelerate the spread of global brand messages into local spaces.

culture-004.zusammenfassung: UNESCO has explicitly identified commercial outdoor advertising as a threat to the visual integrity of World Heritage Sites in its guidelines for sustainable urban management. Several European cities have been called upon to limit OOH (Out-of-Home) advertising in buffer zones.
culture-004.kernbefund: Commercial outdoor advertising in historic city centres and UNESCO buffer zones undermines the authentic visual perception of cultural heritage sites. UNESCO defines "Visual Integrity" as a protected asset: the cityscape should reflect the historical significance of a place — large-scale advertising, particularly DOOH with animated content and night-time illumination, directly conflicts with this protection objective.
culture-004.relevanz: Cities such as Paris, Prague, Vienna, and Florence have introduced OOH advertising restrictions in historic core zones, partly under pressure from UNESCO. In Germany, Nuremberg's old town and Berlin-Mitte are potentially affected as buffer zones of UNESCO sites. Advertising concessions in these areas are subject to increasing legal pressure.

eco-005.zusammenfassung: An analysis of advertisers using outdoor advertising shows that public space surfaces are booked disproportionately often by climate-damaging industries seeking to drive non-sustainable consumption.
eco-005.kernbefund: The most profitable clients for outdoor advertising companies are automobile manufacturers (particularly SUVs), low-cost airlines, fast-food chains, and the fashion industry (Fast Fashion). The constant visual presence of these products in public space cements an extremely resource-intensive lifestyle as a social norm (induced consumption).
eco-005.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is harmful not only through the electricity consumption of the displays themselves (Scope 1/2), but above all through what are known as "Advertised Emissions" (Scope 3) — the greenhouse gases arising from the additional consumption of high-carbon products that are advertised.

eco-006.zusammenfassung: The climate impact of the advertising industry extends far beyond the electricity consumption of screens — it lies in the induced additional consumption of CO2-intensive products.
eco-006.kernbefund: Reports by Purpose Disruptors show that advertising massively increases greenhouse gas emissions from the population by artificially boosting the sale of climate-damaging products (such as SUVs, air travel, or fast food). These "Advertised Emissions" account for a significant share of the ecological footprint of an urban society. Estimates for the UK market show that the additional demand generated by advertising increases emissions by approximately 32%. Outdoor advertising acts here as a "Choice Architect" that normalises climate-damaging lifestyles in public space.
eco-006.relevanz: Advertising companies that describe themselves as "climate-neutral" (by offsetting only the electricity of their screens) ignore the massive Scope 3 effect of the advertised content. This is a form of systemic greenwashing.

eco-007.zusammenfassung: Long-term advertising contracts bind municipalities to private corporations and curtail democratic authority over the design of public space.
eco-007.kernbefund: Cities frequently enter into contracts lasting 15 to 20 years with advertising companies, in which the provision of bus shelters or public toilets is exchanged for exclusive advertising rights. These Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) often develop into debt traps: municipalities lose control over the cityscape and can often only enforce new ecological or social standards (e.g. bans on junk food advertising) by making massive compensation payments to the companies. Furthermore, the locations of the infrastructure often prioritise advertising visibility rather than the needs of citizens, leading to neglect of outlying districts.
eco-007.relevanz: The supposedly "free" infrastructure is purchased at a high price: the loss of political room for manoeuvre and the long-term privatisation of public space.

econ-001.zusammenfassung: Review study on the relationship between income inequality, status-driven consumption, and status anxiety. Shows that advertising promoting status symbols directly contributes to household debt and non-sustainable consumption.
econ-001.kernbefund: Income inequality is associated with higher status-driven consumption and status anxiety. This status anxiety, fuelled by advertising, leads to household debt, spatial inequalities, and non-sustainable consumption behaviour with higher CO₂ emissions.
econ-001.relevanz: Outdoor advertising for luxury goods, status symbols, and aspirationally "upward-oriented" consumer goods reaches all social strata in public space — including those who cannot afford these goods, generating status anxiety and debt particularly among lower-income population groups.

econ-002.zusammenfassung: Econometric study on the relationship between rising income inequality and growing consumer debt. Shows that households with smaller income gains take on debt to maintain their consumption relative to wealthier households.
econ-002.kernbefund: Rising income inequality substantially increases consumer debt. Households with smaller income gains take on debt to emulate the consumption of wealthier groups — a mechanism that advertising deliberately exploits ("Keeping up with the Joneses").
econ-002.relevanz: Outdoor advertising in public space confronts all income groups with the same consumption incentives. Advertising for high-priced goods in public space is a direct driver of the "keeping up" mechanism that drives households into debt.

econ-003.zusammenfassung: NBER (National Bureau of Economic Research) working paper documenting the long-term correlation between growing income inequality and consumption patterns in the USA since the 1960s. Analyses how marketing and advertising accelerate status-driven consumption.
econ-003.kernbefund: Decades of data confirm the relationship between rising inequality and non-sustainable consumption patterns. Advertising and marketing play a central role in accelerating status-driven consumption that perpetuates inequalities.
econ-003.relevanz: Outdoor advertising has been a driver of these consumption patterns for decades — it is the most visible and most pervasive form of commercial messaging in public space.

econ-004.zusammenfassung: Wharton School of Business research study on the effect of income inequality on conspicuous and inconspicuous consumption. Shows that higher inequality leads to more ostentatious (visible) status consumption — precisely what outdoor advertising for high-priced goods incentivises.
econ-004.kernbefund: Higher inequality increases status-signalling consumption (conspicuous consumption). Advertising for luxury goods and status products in public space deliberately exploits and amplifies this mechanism — it targets all income groups and generates social comparison processes that lead to irrational purchasing decisions.
econ-004.relevanz: Outdoor advertising for premium and status goods is particularly effective in public space because it reaches all social strata and generates social comparisons in a context where poverty and wealth meet directly.

econ-008.zusammenfassung: DOOH (Digital Out-of-Home) hardware (LED screens, control units, power supply) has a real service life of 5–7 years, after which the hardware must be replaced. The disposal costs for electronic waste from commercial signage have so far been largely externalised — onto municipalities, taxpayers, and developing countries.
econ-008.kernbefund: The UN E-Waste Monitor 2020 documents that commercial electronic signage waste is one of the fastest-growing e-waste streams. DOOH hardware contains hazardous substances (lead, mercury in older LEDs, indium) for whose proper disposal no adequate take-back systems exist. Cities and municipalities bear the follow-on costs of advertising installations that are disposed of or illegally abandoned in public space.
econ-008.relevanz: Investors in DOOH infrastructure must factor in disposal costs at the end of the hardware lifecycle. In cities with strict advertising bans (São Paulo, Grenoble), significant dismantling and disposal costs arose. The EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) could in future hold DOOH operators accountable for the full hardware lifecycle impact.

env-001.zusammenfassung: DarkSky International, the leading independent organization for light pollution research, documents the enormous energy consumption of digital billboards and their effects on light pollution and ecosystems.
env-001.kernbefund: Digital billboards consume 30 times more energy than an average American household. Electronic Message Centers (EMCs) emit light in all directions (non-directional), can be 10 times brighter than traditional billboards at night, and contribute to global light pollution, which is increasing by 6% annually. 88% of Europe and 50% of the USA are already experiencing perpetual artificial twilight.
env-001.relevanz: This energy consumption is solely attributable to the purpose of commercial attention capture — it serves no public benefit. The costs (energy, light pollution, CO₂) are externalized onto the general public.

env-002.zusammenfassung: Academic analysis (Journal of Marketing Communications) and corroborating data from The Drum show: the digital advertising industry emits 7.2 million tonnes of CO₂ per year — more than the entire aviation industry. DOOH contributes to this through both direct energy consumption (screens, servers) and indirect emissions generated by consumption incentives.
env-002.kernbefund: The digital advertising industry emits 7.2 million tonnes of CO₂ per year — equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of 1.4 million US households and an estimated 1.7% of global greenhouse gas emissions by 2025 (aviation: 1.9%). A single digital advertising campaign generates approximately 70 tonnes of CO₂e — the annual emissions of 7 people. In addition, there are massive indirect emissions: online advertising accounts for 10–20% of total internet infrastructure energy consumption; DOOH combines both effects.
env-002.relevanz: Digital out-of-home advertising is the fastest-growing segment of outdoor advertising. Every new DOOH billboard amplifies this emissions load — 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, for commercial purposes without democratic legitimacy in public space. The 7.2 million tonne figure covers all digital advertising channels; DOOH makes a disproportionate contribution due to its 24/7 operation.

env-003.zusammenfassung: The first systematic assessment of the environmental costs of digital advertising campaigns using life cycle analyses. Quantifies energy consumption and CO₂ emissions per ad placement.
env-003.kernbefund: Digital advertising causes measurable and quantifiable environmental costs that have so far not been taken into account in any regulation. The study provides a methodology for calculating the ecological footprint of advertising campaigns — outdoor advertising with continuously operating screens is particularly cost-intensive.
env-003.relevanz: DOOH screens run 24/7 in public spaces without any possibility for citizens to switch them off. The environmental costs are externalized and borne by society, while the profits accrue privately.

env-004.zusammenfassung: Light from digital billboards and illuminated outdoor advertising affects the behavior of nocturnal animals and disrupts biological rhythms in both humans and animals. Global light pollution is increasing by 6% annually.
env-004.kernbefund: Artificial light from billboards disrupts the reproduction, foraging, and orientation of nocturnal animals: birds, bats, frogs, and insects become disoriented or are directly harmed. For humans: excessive artificial light at night leads to sleep disorders, endocrine disruptions, and increased cancer risk (melatonin suppression).
env-004.relevanz: Billboards are frequently positioned and illuminated to maximize visibility — not to minimize environmental impact. 88% of Europe already suffers from light pollution. Advertising is a substantial and avoidable share of this burden.

env-005.zusammenfassung: Research by the Leibniz-Institut für Gewässerökologie und Binnenfischerei (IGB) (Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries), Berlin, demonstrates a clear causal link between light pollution and the decline of flying insects. Regions with severe insect decline also show high levels of light pollution.
env-005.kernbefund: In regions with severe declines in flying insects, levels of light pollution are also high. IGB researchers found strong evidence for a causal relationship. Artificial light at night disrupts the reproduction, foraging, and orientation of insects.
env-005.relevanz: Illuminated billboards, and especially digital DOOH screens, are — after street lighting — one of the most common sources of artificial light in urban and peri-urban (semi-urban) spaces. Billboards illuminate 24/7 — including during hours when street lighting is dimmed.

env-006.zusammenfassung: Research by the Senckenberg Gesellschaft für Naturforschung (Senckenberg Society for Nature Research), Frankfurt, on the molecular effects of light pollution on insects. For the first time, the extent to which artificial light at night influences the gene expression of insects was demonstrated.
env-006.kernbefund: Artificial light at night causes profound changes in the gene expression of insects: 1,564 genes were affected in midge larvae (Chironomidae). The consequences include delayed development, increased oxidative stress, and drastically reduced reproductive capacity. This threatens the entire food chain, as insects form the foundation for birds, fish, and other animals.
env-006.relevanz: Billboards are one of the few light sources in public space that serve exclusively commercial purposes. Unlike street lights, they have no safety function. The ecological damage caused by advertising illumination is avoidable.

env-007.zusammenfassung: A comprehensive analysis by the Bayerische Akademie für Naturschutz und Landschaftspflege (ANL Bayern) (Bavarian Academy for Nature Conservation and Landscape Management) on light pollution as a factor in insect decline. This state Bavarian authority officially documents the connection.
env-007.kernbefund: Light pollution is a significant factor in insect decline. The study analyzes all relevant types of lighting in urban and rural spaces. Billboards are explicitly identified as a relevant light source.
env-007.relevanz: This is an official report from a Bavarian state authority. It demonstrates that the legislature recognizes light pollution as an environmental problem — and implicitly that commercial lighting (billboards) is part of the problem.

env-008.zusammenfassung: The 'Badvertising' campaign documents that advertising for high-emission products (such as SUVs and short-haul flights) directly benefits sales figures and thus CO₂ emissions, drawing parallels to tobacco advertising.
env-008.kernbefund: Despite massive efforts toward climate protection, outdoor advertising actively drives the sale of particularly climate-damaging SUVs. The report argues that a transport transition (shift away from car dependency) is impossible as long as public space is used to promote the most harmful modes of transport.
env-008.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is not climate-neutral — it is an active driver of the climate crisis as long as high-carbon products are permitted to be advertised.

env-009.zusammenfassung: The Landesamt für Natur, Umwelt und Verbraucherschutz NRW (LANUV) (State Office for Nature, Environment and Consumer Protection of North Rhine-Westphalia) conducted a state-wide survey of sky glow in NRW. Commercial outdoor lighting and illuminated advertising are identified as significant emission factors.
env-009.kernbefund: The technical report and the associated guidelines (the 'Licht-Erlass' NRW, i.e., the NRW Light Ordinance) show that artificial outdoor lighting — including intensely luminous DOOH installations — contributes to massive disruptions of human biorhythms and to insect decline. The authority recommends strict limits on luminance levels and nighttime switch-offs to reduce emissions.
env-009.relevanz: State environmental authorities in densely populated federal states such as NRW officially recognize outdoor advertising as a serious source of environmental and health-damaging emissions that requires stricter regulation.

env-010.zusammenfassung: The technological shift from traditional 'illuminated surfaces' (backlit paper) to digital LED screens (DOOH) represents a drastic worsening of light emissions.
env-010.kernbefund: A traditional City Light Poster (a backlit static advertising poster common in German cities) illuminates passively, with fluorescent light filtered through printed paper. A digital DOOH screen, however, consists of thousands of tiny LED lamps that emit light directly (and often non-directionally) into the surroundings. To be visible in daylight, LEDs radiate extremely brightly (up to 7,000 nits). Even in dimmed night mode, they contribute massively to sky glow (Skyglow) due to the blue-heavy LED spectrum.
env-010.relevanz: Cities that permit digital screens are not simply swapping one advertising format for another. They are authorizing the construction of massive, active light sources that demonstrably disrupt sleep cycles (circadian rhythm) and decimate insect populations.

env-011.zusammenfassung: The expansion of Digital Out-of-Home (DOOH) is increasingly running up against the hard limits of national environmental and nature conservation law in Germany.
env-011.kernbefund: In Germany, the Lichtimmissionsrichtlinie (LAI) (Light Emission Guideline), based on the Bundes-Immissionsschutzgesetz (BImSchG) (Federal Immission Control Act), stipulates strict limit values for harmful environmental effects caused by light. DOOH screens, which can reach up to 10,000 nits of brightness, frequently exceed these tolerance values with regard to glare effects on traffic and 'room brightening' in bedrooms. Furthermore, the new German Insektenschutzgesetz (Insect Protection Act) and amendments to the Bundesnaturschutzgesetz BNatSchG (Federal Nature Conservation Act) prohibit the installation of lighting systems in certain nature conservation areas and mandate massively reduced light emissions at night, as artificial LED light (particularly in the blue spectrum emitted by DOOH) decimates nocturnal insect populations (the 'vacuum cleaner effect').
env-011.relevanz: The advertising industry is coming under massive legal pressure from environmental protection law. From an immission control perspective, DOOH is a significant, and often impermissible, environmental burden.

env-012.zusammenfassung: The extreme brightness of digital advertising installations at night disrupts the biological rhythms and migration routes of protected bird species.
env-012.kernbefund: Scientific studies in Europe show that large-format, high-brightness LED screens (particularly those with a high blue-light component) contribute to 'Skyglow' during nighttime hours, which disorients migratory birds. Birds are attracted to the light sources (phototaxis), leading to fatal collisions with buildings or to exhaustion caused by unnecessary detours. Since many European metropolises lie along major migration routes, the unfiltered light emission from DOOH poses a direct threat to biodiversity and undermines urban efforts for species conservation.
env-012.relevanz: DOOH is not a 'clean' technology. The ecological costs from species loss and disrupted ecosystems are systematically excluded from the sustainability reports of advertising corporations.

env-013.zusammenfassung: The 'digitalization' of outdoor advertising generates enormous quantities of difficult-to-recycle electronic waste (e-waste) and consumes critical raw materials.
env-013.kernbefund: Unlike analogue billboards, which can last for decades, digital LED screens have a short technical and economic lifespan of often only 5 to 8 years. Rapid technological progress and LED degradation lead to frequent 'hardware upgrades.' This generates tonnes of e-waste containing rare earth elements, lead, and cadmium. Studies show that recycling these complex electronic components is extremely energy-intensive, and disposal often takes place in countries of the Global South under precarious conditions, causing severe soil and water contamination.
env-013.relevanz: The industry promotes the 'paperless' future as ecologically beneficial, but conceals the massive environmental burden caused by the production and disposal of the hardware. DOOH is a disposable technology deployed in public space.

env-014.zusammenfassung: PVC advertising banner materials — the standard material for large-format advertising — weather under UV radiation and mechanical abrasion into microplastic particles that enter soils, drainage systems, and waterways. In urban areas with a high density of OOH (out-of-home) advertising, this input pathway is significant.
env-014.kernbefund: PVC advertising banners (standard advertising material) contain plasticizers such as DEHP (endocrine-disrupting) and stabilizers such as lead and cadmium. UV weathering produces microplastic particles < 5mm that enter urban stormwater runoff. Urban stormwater runoff transports microplastics directly into waterways — wastewater treatment filters out less than 60%.
env-014.relevanz: In Germany, advertising banners are replaced every 4 weeks (campaign cycle). Even prior to replacement, existing banners contribute to microplastic pollution through weathering. The problem is only partially addressed by the increasing prevalence of DOOH (which displaces static posters) — DOOH hardware itself contains considerable quantities of plastics (housings, cables, circuit boards).

env-015.zusammenfassung: The Otto Brenner Stiftung (Otto Brenner Foundation) and the University of Leipzig analyzed 9,779 advertising spots from German TV channels and YouTube. Result: **30.3% of all advertising spots** promote climate-damaging products and services — and in the assessment of the researchers, thereby violate the Medienstaatsvertrag (Interstate Media Treaty), which prohibits advertising for highly environmentally harmful behavior.
env-015.kernbefund: 9,779 spots were manually coded (approx. 52 hours of video material). **Every third spot** advertises climate killers — primarily automobiles, aviation, and food. Particularly absurd according to the study: advertising for climate-damaging products frequently conveys the message that one is doing something good for the environment (greenwashing). The study authors call for strict regulation or a complete advertising ban for climate-damaging product categories. Although the study examines TV and YouTube, the product categories (cars, flights, fossil energy) apply equally to OOH/DOOH advertising.
env-015.relevanz: DOOH networks in Germany generate considerable revenue from the same product categories: automobiles, energy, food/fast food. The Medienstaatsvertrag (Interstate Media Treaty) applies to broadcasting — a corresponding regulation for outdoor advertising does not yet exist. However, the study provides the scientific basis for extending the prohibition to OOH/DOOH, as demanded by, among others, Badvertising (UK) and the Initiative Fossil Werbung Abschaffen (Abolish Fossil Advertising Initiative) (DE).

env-016.zusammenfassung: In September 2022, Germany's Energiesparverordnung (Energy Saving Ordinance) came into force, requiring illuminated outdoor advertising to be switched off between 22:00 and 16:00. The OOH industry itself estimated the annual energy consumption of digital advertising installations in Germany at **113,000 MWh** — equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of approximately 40,000 two-person households. The federal government responded to the energy crisis with a nationwide switch-off requirement; the outdoor advertising industry described the measure as 'incomprehensible' and criticized 'loopholes.'
env-016.kernbefund: The figure cited by the OOH industry association itself — 113,000 MWh/year for digital outdoor advertising in Germany alone — is an industry-acknowledged measure of resource consumption. This energy requirement serves exclusively the monetization of public attention; it provides no basic supply function, no public benefit. The federal government classified it as dispensable within the framework of energy security — the first nationwide state qualification of DOOH operation as non-essential energy consumption.
env-016.relevanz: The Energiesparverordnung (Energy Saving Ordinance) is the most direct regulatory signal from the German federal government against DOOH operation. At the same time, the industry's own figure (113,000 MWh/year) demonstrates the scale of energy consumption: DOOH networks in Germany consume more electricity than 40,000 households — for purely advertising purposes. With rising energy prices and climate protection targets, further regulatory pressure on the operation of digital screens in public space is foreseeable.

equity-001.zusammenfassung: Study on the distribution of harmful product advertising (alcohol, unhealthy food, gambling) in public space and on school routes. Also analyzes the effectiveness of advertising bans.
equity-001.kernbefund: Children are systematically exposed to advertising for harmful products on their way to school. Advertising along home-to-school routes reinforces messages through repetition. Neighborhoods with particularly high exposure show elevated health risks. Voluntary bans are ineffective — only mandatory government regulations show measurable impact.
equity-001.relevanz: Children have no control over what advertising they are exposed to on their daily routes. This is a structural violation of their protection — a public space that daily confronts children with alcohol, junk food, and gambling advertising fails in its duty as a safe environment.

equity-002.zusammenfassung: Environmental justice (the fair distribution of environmental benefits and burdens) study in Los Angeles on the spatial inequality of harmful outdoor advertising (alcohol, tobacco, junk food). Reveals structural racism and class inequality in the placement of outdoor advertising.
equity-002.kernbefund: Low-income neighborhoods and neighborhoods with a high proportion of people of color bear a disproportionately high burden of harmful outdoor advertising. The distribution is not random but follows patterns that correlate with existing social inequalities — outdoor advertising reinforces and perpetuates these inequalities.
equity-002.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is not a neutral medium — it is strategically placed so that vulnerable groups are disproportionately exposed. This is a form of structural discrimination by commercial interests in public space.

equity-003.zusammenfassung: A comprehensive study in the United Kingdom shows that commercial outdoor advertising appears up to six times more frequently in low-income areas than in affluent neighborhoods.
equity-003.kernbefund: The report "Unavoidable Impact" documents that people in poorer neighborhoods are not only more frequently exposed to advertising for junk food, alcohol, and gambling, but also suffer more severely from visual pollution and light pollution (DOOH). Affluent residential areas often successfully repel advertising billboards.
equity-003.relevanz: Outdoor advertising intensifies social and health inequalities (environmental justice) by systematically targeting vulnerable population groups.

equity-004.zusammenfassung: The modernization of advertising infrastructure in the Global North leads to the export of ecologically harmful and inefficient hardware to developing countries.
equity-004.kernbefund: When advertising companies in Europe or North America upgrade their inventory to the latest, more energy-efficient LED generation, the old, power-hungry, and often maintenance-intensive panels are frequently exported as "second-hand hardware" to countries in the Global South. There, these installations contribute to overloading local power grids and end up on informal waste dumps at the end of their lifecycle. This phenomenon is criticized as "eco-colonialism" (the externalization of environmental costs onto less powerful nations): the Global North "cleans up" its urban footprint while the ecological and energy-related damage is offloaded to countries with weaker environmental laws.
equity-004.relevanz: The industry's sustainability reports are often geographically selective. The global hardware footprint is obscured by externalizing the harmful part of the value chain (disposal/dumping).

health-001.zusammenfassung: Systematic review study on outdoor food advertising: reach, effectiveness, and impacts on eating behavior and health. Published in BMC Public Health, Springer Nature.
health-001.kernbefund: Outdoor food advertising is as extensive and effective as digital or TV advertising. Skepticism among adolescents does not protect against its effects. Both young children and older adolescents are susceptible. Evidence shows that advertising influences dietary preferences and consumption patterns.
health-001.relevanz: Unlike TV or online, outdoor advertising for unhealthy food cannot be switched off, clicked away, or filtered. Children are exposed to it along their entire school route — in a context where no parental supervision or guidance is possible.

health-002.zusammenfassung: Canadian cross-sectional study that establishes for the first time a direct correlation between exposure to outdoor food advertising and the actual purchasing behavior of adolescents. Peer-reviewed, published in Oxford Health Promotion International.
health-002.kernbefund: The study demonstrates a statistically significant direct correlation between the frequency of exposure to outdoor food advertising and the purchasing behavior of adolescents. More advertising = more purchases of the advertised (predominantly unhealthy) products.
health-002.relevanz: This study provides the most direct causal evidence: outdoor food advertising measurably changes the purchasing behavior of adolescents. Published in 2024 — this is current, reliable evidence.

health-003.zusammenfassung: Cross-sectional study quantifying the relationship between the density of food advertising in a neighborhood and the residents' risk of overweight. Published in BMC Public Health.
health-003.kernbefund: A higher proportion of food advertising in neighborhoods is associated with increased rates of overweight and obesity. For every 10% increase in the share of food advertising, the risk of overweight rises by a factor of 1.05. The effect is measurable at the neighborhood level and is statistically significant.
health-003.relevanz: This study directly quantifies the health damage from outdoor food advertising at the population level. It shows that the placement of advertising in public space has measurable public health consequences.

health-004.zusammenfassung: WHO guideline and ELENA (e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions) intervention on food marketing to children. The WHO recommends binding legislative measures to protect children from marketing for foods high in saturated fats, trans fats, free sugars, and salt.
health-004.kernbefund: Voluntary self-regulatory commitments by the advertising industry are demonstrably ineffective. The WHO calls for binding, state-enforced restrictions — including for outdoor advertising — because otherwise children are left defenseless against aggressive marketing.
health-004.relevanz: The WHO explicitly names outdoor advertising as one of the channels that must be regulated. This is one of the highest international health authorities classifying outdoor advertising targeting children as harmful to health.

health-005.zusammenfassung: Peer-reviewed study in Prevention Science (Springer) analyzing harmful marketing as an overlooked social determinant of health. Examines 6 industries: tobacco, alcohol, pharmaceuticals, processed foods, firearms, and fossil fuels.
health-005.kernbefund: Marketing across 6 industries is causally responsible for disease and death. More than 1 million Americans die annually from the consequences of products promoted through marketing. The study frames harmful marketing as a structural public health determinant — comparable to poverty or lack of education.
health-005.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is the most visible and universally accessible channel for precisely these harmful products (alcohol, tobacco, unhealthy food). In public space, exposure is unavoidable — especially for vulnerable groups (children, people with addiction disorders).

health-006.zusammenfassung: Study by the University of Hamburg, commissioned by the Deutsche Allianz Nichtübertragbare Krankheiten (DANK — German Alliance for Non-Communicable Diseases) and the AOK-Bundesverband (national health insurer federation). Systematically analyzes food advertising directed at children in Germany.
health-006.kernbefund: A child between 3 and 13 years of age in Germany sees an average of 15 food advertisements for unhealthy products per day (5 online, 10 on television). 92% of all food advertisements directed at children concern unhealthy products (89% on TV, 98% online).
health-006.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is part of the same advertising ecosystem that generates this systematic exposure of children to unhealthy food. On the school route, at bus stops, and in shopping zones, children are exposed to the same brand messages — without parental supervision and without the ability to switch off.

health-007.zusammenfassung: DFG (Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft — German Research Foundation)-funded FAIR project (Fraunhofer ISI, Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences, University of Mannheim) examining the impact of influencer marketing on adolescents in Germany. Survey of more than 1,000 adolescents.
health-007.kernbefund: Approximately 50% of surveyed adolescents had purchased products advertised by influencers. More than half had spent over 50 euros on influencer-promoted products within 6 months. Adolescents are particularly vulnerable due to intensive social media use and less developed advertising literacy.
health-007.relevanz: Influencer marketing and outdoor advertising are part of the same advertising system. Both exploit similar psychological mechanisms (parasocial relationships, attention capture, status appeals). The vulnerability of adolescents to advertising messages in public space is analogous to their susceptibility to influencer marketing.

health-008.zusammenfassung: The omnipresence of sports betting and gambling advertising at bus stops and on billboards is identified by public health experts as a major driver of addictive behavior.
health-008.kernbefund: Outdoor advertising for gambling normalizes risky behavior, triggers relapse in recovered problem gamblers, and introduces adolescents to sports betting at an early age. Unlike TV advertising, vulnerable individuals cannot avoid advertising in public space — for example, on the way to school or work.
health-008.relevanz: Outdoor advertising acts as a direct multiplier of health and financial crises for vulnerable groups through the aggressive promotion of addictive products (alongside alcohol, also gambling).

health-009.zusammenfassung: Scientific studies document the massive positive effect of advertising restrictions on public health.
health-009.kernbefund: A comprehensive study by LSHTM (London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine) and the University of Sheffield examined the 2019 ban on advertising for products high in fat, sugar, and salt (HFSS — High in Fat, Sugar and Salt) across the London transport network (TfL — Transport for London). The result: the ban led to a reduction in weekly energy intake from HFSS products of an average of 6.7% per household. This corresponds to a long-term prevention of an estimated 94,867 obesity cases and nearly 3,000 cases of type 2 diabetes in London. In addition, the British health system (NHS) is saving costs exceeding £200 million as a result.
health-009.relevanz: This is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that outdoor advertising is not mere information but directly influences the eating behavior of an entire city of millions. Advertising bans are a highly effective preventive medicine measure.

health-010.zusammenfassung: In Germany, the school is legally enshrined as an advertising-free protected space in order to preserve pedagogical integrity and pupils' independence.
health-010.kernbefund: As a representative example, § 99 of the Schulgesetz NRW (School Act for the State of North Rhine-Westphalia) stipulates that advertising that does not serve educational purposes is generally prohibited on school premises. This encompasses both the distribution of materials and the posting of posters on school grounds. The aim is to protect minors during a sensitive phase of development from the influence of commercial actors and to ensure that school remains a place of critical reflection rather than unfiltered consumption. Sponsoring is only permitted under the strictest conditions, with the advertising effect required to "clearly take a back seat to the educational benefit."
health-010.relevanz: If the state protects schools as advertising-free zones, the ethical question arises as to why the same protection for children in the immediate vicinity of schools (at bus stops and on school routes) is systematically undermined by commercial OOH (out-of-home) installations.

health-011.zusammenfassung: Nighttime illumination from digital advertising displays directly interferes with the hormonal regulation of the human sleep-wake cycle.
health-011.kernbefund: Digital advertising screens use LEDs that often operate at very high color temperatures (above 6,500 Kelvin), which emit a high proportion of blue light. This short-wave light suppresses the release of melatonin in the pineal gland — a hormone essential for sleep and cellular regeneration. Residents in urban areas whose windows are lit up by DOOH (Digital Out-of-Home) screens suffer from a chronic shift in their circadian rhythm. The American Medical Association (AMA) warns of long-term consequences such as sleep disorders, metabolic diseases, and an increased risk of certain cancers caused by ALAN (Artificial Light at Night).
health-011.relevanz: DOOH operators often argue in terms of brightness per surface area, but ignore the biological potency of color temperature. The nighttime emission of blue light is a massive intrusion on the physical integrity of residents.

health-012.zusammenfassung: Peer-reviewed longitudinal study examining the relationship between the density of outdoor alcohol advertising near schools and alcohol consumption as well as consumption intentions among adolescents.
health-012.kernbefund: Adolescents in neighborhoods with a high density of outdoor alcohol advertising show significantly higher intentions to consume alcohol and report higher actual consumption. Outdoor alcohol advertising near schools and residential areas acts as an independent risk factor — more potent than TV advertising, because it cannot be avoided.
health-012.relevanz: Outdoor alcohol advertising is largely legal and unregulated in Germany. The WHO has called for mandatory restrictions on alcohol marketing in public places. Unlike TV advertising (restricted after 10 p.m.), OOH is visible around the clock — including to children on their school route.

health-013.zusammenfassung: A systematic umbrella review (2023, Public Health journal) synthesized 8 systematic reviews covering a combined total of 74 individual studies. Result: there is consistent evidence of a **causal relationship** between gambling advertising and more positive attitudes toward gambling as well as increased willingness to gamble — with a clear **dose-response effect**. Children, adolescents, and already at-risk individuals are most severely affected. 1 in 7 UK gambling advertisements contained no age warning whatsoever; 84% of warning labels and 54% of harm-minimization messages had very low visibility.
health-013.kernbefund: The causal relationship is established on the basis of 74 studies — significantly more evidence than exists for most regulated product categories. The dose-response relationship means: the more advertising, the stronger the effect. OOH (out-of-home advertising) is particularly critical because children cannot avoid it. Existing self-regulatory measures (warning labels) are demonstrably ineffective.
health-013.relevanz: Gambling advertising is one of the most important revenue categories for DOOH networks in Europe. The evidence clearly demonstrates: OOH gambling advertising causes measurable, dose-dependent harm — particularly to children on school routes and low-income population groups who are disproportionately exposed. Regulatory bodies in the UK, Belgium, and Spain have already enacted restrictions; Germany is under increasing political pressure.

pol-001.zusammenfassung: The outdoor advertising market is heavily monopolized. A small number of large corporations (JCDecaux, Clear Channel, Ströer, Wall GmbH, Outfront Media) control the majority of advertising spaces in public areas worldwide.
pol-001.kernbefund: This oligopoly position enables these corporations to exert enormous political and economic pressure on municipalities (local governments). Local and small businesses can often not afford advertising space in city centers, meaning that public space primarily carries messages from global brands.
pol-001.relevanz: The dominance of the "big players" leads to a commercialization of public space in which democratic control and local economic structures are weakened.

pol-002.zusammenfassung: Cities increasingly no longer finance public infrastructure (such as bus shelters and public toilets) from tax revenues, but instead hand over their provision to advertising corporations in exchange for long-term advertising rights.
pol-002.kernbefund: These contracts, often concluded for 10 to 15 years, bind municipalities to the advertising industry over the long term. They make it legally difficult or impossible for cities to subsequently regulate or ban outdoor advertising for climate protection or health reasons. JCDecaux and Ströer are pioneers in this model.
pol-002.relevanz: Public space loses its neutrality. Street furniture (Stadtmobiliar) is designed and positioned primarily as an advertising medium, rather than according to the actual needs of citizens.

pol-003.zusammenfassung: The advertising industry invests considerable sums in lobbying at the municipal and national level to prevent or weaken regulations on DOOH (Digital Out of Home) screens.
pol-003.kernbefund: Reports from NGOs such as Corporate Europe Observatory show that outdoor advertisers systematically exert pressure to obtain exemptions from light emission laws (e.g., mandatory shutdown at night) and restrictions on advertising for unhealthy products. The argument frequently made is the alleged financial dependence of municipalities on advertising revenues.
pol-003.relevanz: The political influence of the big players means that health and environmental policy measures to protect citizens are blocked in favor of corporate profits.

pol-004.zusammenfassung: The Cologne (NRW)-based outdoor advertising giant Ströer SE & Co. KGaA uses its financial power and direct political lobbying to secure exclusive, long-term concessions for advertising space on public land.
pol-004.kernbefund: Investigations by investigative NGOs such as Correctiv show that the company's market power is so great that cities effectively have no real alternatives when awarding street furniture contracts (bus shelters). Ströer is also officially registered in the Lobbyregister (the federal lobbying register) and exerts direct influence on urban development policy matters and data protection guidelines.
pol-004.relevanz: The massive local entrenchment of advertising corporations creates a dependency among municipalities. Democratic shaping of public space is undermined by economic monopolies.

pol-005.zusammenfassung: Citizens are increasingly and successfully pushing back against the privatization of public space by outdoor advertising, by strategically using planning and building regulations.
pol-005.kernbefund: Local grassroots organizations (such as the Adblock network in the UK or Résistance à l'Agression Publicitaire (Resistance to Advertising Aggression) in France) systematically monitor municipal planning portals for new applications for DOOH screens and billboards. By mobilizing large numbers of residents and submitting well-founded objections (based on traffic safety, light pollution, and heritage protection), these groups regularly force advertising corporations to withdraw planning applications, or secure rejections from urban planning authorities.
pol-005.relevanz: The advertising industry no longer encounters passive acceptance, but rather organized, informed, and legally effective democratic resistance from civil society.

pol-006.zusammenfassung: The commercialization of public space is encountering massive democratic resistance in Germany, which has manifested in formal legislative procedures.
pol-006.kernbefund: The citizens' initiative "Berlin Werbefrei" (Berlin Ad-Free) collected over 36,000 valid signatures in the first stage of a Volksbegehren (citizens' referendum process) in order to introduce its own far-reaching legislative draft into the Berlin Abgeordnetenhaus (state parliament). The draft envisions radically banning product and consumer advertising in Berlin's public space. Only advertising at the point of sale (e.g., the sign above a bakery), event announcements, and public interest information would remain permitted.
pol-006.relevanz: This initiative proves that a strong, enfranchised civil society rejects the constant visual pressure to consume. Outdoor advertising is increasingly perceived not as harmless decoration, but as a psychological intrusion into public space.

pol-007.zusammenfassung: The aggressive expansion of commercial advertising space is depriving the local arts scene and civic movements of the physical space for non-commercial forms of expression.
pol-007.kernbefund: In many major cities, facades that were previously free or used for community murals (wall paintings) are being taken over by large-format advertising banners or digital screens. This process leads to a cultural homogenization: instead of locally rooted, political or aesthetic art, interchangeable global brand messages appear. Sociological studies show that this weakens residents' identification with their neighborhood, since public space is no longer perceived as a place for co-creation but as a pure consumption zone. The city's "canvas" is sold to the highest bidder instead of serving as a stage for local culture.
pol-007.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is an active displacement factor for non-commercial culture. It replaces diversity with monotony and civic participation with one-directional messaging.

pol-008.zusammenfassung: Berlin sold its advertising rights in public street space in 2018: for the next 15 years (from 2019), the state collects 350 million euros from advertising corporations. Berlin is the most heavily commercialized outdoor advertising city in Germany — 18.5% of total German OOH advertising revenues flow through a single city.
pol-008.kernbefund:
Berlin has **20,643 advertising surfaces** that generate annual poster revenues of **272 million euros**. This represents 18.5% of all German outdoor advertising revenues. The rights were awarded in lots to Wall/JCDecaux (169 large-format illuminated panels + 883 display cases), ILG-Außenwerbung (2,500 Litfaßsäulen (round advertising columns)), Mediateam Stadtservice (4,100 poster sites), and Ströer (430 clock locations). Contract terms: 10–15 years.

The previous model of "infrastructure in exchange for advertising rights" (Wall maintained public toilets and fountains in exchange for advertising space) was replaced by direct payments — with the consequence that the Senate must now fund this infrastructure itself.
pol-008.relevanz: Exclusive contracts of 10–15 years with corporations such as JCDecaux/Wall and Ströer mean: democratically elected city councils cannot, for the duration of these contracts, reduce the number of advertising surfaces, enforce bans on specific product categories, or stop the expansion to digital screens — without risking contractual penalties. Public space is commercially locked up for 15 years.

pol-009.zusammenfassung: Investigative research by CORRECTIV, ZDF Frontal, and Der Spiegel: Between 2016 and 2018, more than 9,400 large-format posters for the AfD (Alternative für Deutschland, a right-wing political party) were booked in approximately 70 German cities via Ströer's booking system — paid for by anonymous donors for over 3 million euros. The AfD was registered in the booking system as a "direct customer." Ströer left the catalogue of questions unanswered.
pol-009.kernbefund: The investigation documents: **over 3 million euros** of anonymous campaign support for the AfD via Ströer surfaces, of which 1.9 million euros were for the 2017 federal election (Bundestagswahl) (approx. 4,900 posters), 521,000 euros for the NRW state election (Landtagswahl), and 221,000 euros for Baden-Württemberg. Party law expert Sophie Schönberger stated: *"We now have proof that the campaign was coordinated at least at the level of the poster producer"* — a possible illegal party donation structure. Ströer regarded itself as a "neutral service provider" and refused to comment.
pol-009.relevanz: Ströer operates advertising surfaces in over 1,200 German cities on the basis of municipal exclusive contracts. As a de facto monopolist for outdoor advertising in many municipalities, the corporation controls which political content is visible in public space — without parliamentary oversight or transparency obligations. The company also owns Statista (a data service) and t-online (a news portal), which extends its influence over public opinion beyond its physical advertising infrastructure.

pol-010.zusammenfassung: Documentation of the creeping commercialization of public space in Hanover (Hannover) by Ströer (subsidiary DSM — Deutsche Städte Medien GmbH): Between 2014 and 2021, Ströer tripled its advertising infrastructure in the city. The city refuses to provide information about contract details, claiming that the companies themselves should communicate their plans.
pol-010.kernbefund:
Ströer's presence in Hanover in 2021 (according to the investigation): **90 City-Star columns, 1,200 large-format posters, 350 Mega-Light installations** (growth from 70 to 210 = ×3 since 2014), **2,200 City-Light post boxes, 11 LED billboards, 200 clock locations, 350 traditional Litfaßsäulen (round advertising columns)**. Origin: In 2009, DSM received approval for 7 City-Star systems in exchange for free election poster spaces at 45 locations. From those 7, the number grew to over 90.

When asked about contract details, the city's press spokesperson replied: *"Companies should communicate their own plans."*
pol-010.relevanz: The Hanover pattern is exemplary for Germany: small initial contract → creeping expansion → monopoly position → opaque contract terms → democratically uncontrollable expansion. Municipalities successively lose control over how their public space is commercially used, because contract details are protected as trade secrets.

pol-011.zusammenfassung: Hamburg sold its public space advertising rights for 508 million euros to JCDecaux and Ströer following a Europe-wide tender in 2007/2009. JCDecaux received approximately 2,150 bus shelters (Fahrgastunterstände) and 350 city information systems (Stadtinformationsanlagen) (2009–2024). The contracts are publicly accessible in Hamburg's Transparenzportal (Transparency Portal) — one of the few German cities that publishes contract details.
pol-011.kernbefund: Hamburg guaranteed advertising corporations **508 million euros** in advertising revenues over the contract term in exchange for street furniture. Although the contracts stipulated that advertising systems were to be integrated into bus shelters, freestanding advertising systems flooded the cityscape — at nearly every major intersection in prominent locations. The Hamburgisches Transparenzportal (Hamburg Transparency Portal) publishes the contract documents for both lots (JCDecaux Lot 1: city information systems; JCDecaux Lot 2: 18/1 large-format advertising installations).
pol-011.relevanz: Hamburg is one of the rare cases in Germany where contract details are publicly accessible. The 508-million-euro guarantee shows: cities effectively grant monopoly rights over their public space in exchange for revenues. During the contract term (15 years), no advertising bans for specific product categories (e.g., fossil fuels, alcohol, junk food) can be imposed without risking contractual penalties. Democratic city politics is circumvented by commercial contract logic.

pol-012.zusammenfassung: In April 2016, the US short-seller Muddy Waters Research (known for uncovering accounting scandals at Chinese companies) published a report accusing Ströer SE & Co. KGaA of serious IFRS violations. The Ströer share price lost over 25% of its value within 45 minutes of publication (falling from €52 to below €35).
pol-012.kernbefund: Muddy Waters claimed that Ströer's reported organic growth, EBITDA, operating cash flow, and free cash flow were **substantially lower than reported** and violated IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) accounting standards — creating the false impression that the company was financing itself from its own resources. Specifically: digital organic growth rates were allegedly presented in a manipulated manner. Ströer rejected all allegations; the Frankfurt public prosecutor's office subsequently investigated Muddy Waters for possible market manipulation. WirtschaftsWoche (a German business weekly) reported again in 2021 on "suspicious financial conduct" by the corporation.
pol-012.relevanz: Ströer, as Germany's largest outdoor advertiser, operates municipal exclusive contracts in over 1,200 cities. Investors and municipalities entering into long-term partnerships with the corporation face a documented transparency problem: both the financial reporting (Muddy Waters 2016, WirtschaftsWoche 2021) and the political influence (AfD donation scandal 2021) reveal a company that systematically avoids oversight and accountability.

pol-013.zusammenfassung: Jean-Claude Decaux, founder and chairman of JCDecaux, was convicted by the Tribunal de Bordeaux (Bordeaux Criminal Court, France) for "favoritisme" (favoritism/cronyism) and corruption in the awarding of public contracts. The trigger: a contract worth 39.8 million francs (approx. 6 million euros) for school clocks in 204 schools of the Aquitaine Regional Council was awarded without competitive tender to a Decaux subsidiary. Senator Jacques Verlade was convicted of bribery. Decaux received a six-month suspended sentence and a fine of 100,000 francs. He lodged an appeal.
pol-013.kernbefund: The case documents the direct personal involvement of the JCDecaux group chairman in the manipulation of public procurement procedures. Instead of a competitive tender, a Decaux company obtained the contract through personal relationships with an elected politician. The criminal court found the award to be unlawful and issued convictions.
pol-013.relevanz: JCDecaux is the world's largest OOH corporation and is involved in hundreds of municipal exclusive contracts across Europe. The criminal conviction of the founder for manipulation of public procurement procedures is paradigmatic for the business model: cities are dependent on the corporation's contracting practices, and oversight by public institutions has proved inadequate. This case is the earliest documented criminal offense in the company's history.

pol-014.zusammenfassung: FragDenStaat (a German freedom-of-information platform, comparable to "Ask the State") filed a freedom of information request for the disclosure of advertising rights contracts between the BVG (Berliner Verkehrsbetriebe, Berlin's public transport operator) and Wall GmbH (a JCDecaux subsidiary) as well as Ströer. The Berlin Administrative Court ruled in 2019: the financial terms of the contracts do not have to be disclosed — even though the contracts themselves contained a clause stating they held "no trade secrets." The court nonetheless weighed JCDecaux's interest in confidentiality more heavily than the public interest in transparency.
pol-014.kernbefund: The public finances public infrastructure through taxes (BVG buses, trams, metro stations), on which JCDecaux exclusively places advertising. The precise financial terms — that is, how much the city receives for the use of its infrastructure — remain secret. The only publicly known figure: BVG advertising revenues amounted to approximately 10 million euros per year according to the authority's own statements. JCDecaux's original bid from 2006 is reported to have been 103 million euros over the contract term. The contract was renewed in 2021 for a further five years without a public tender.
pol-014.relevanz: The Berlin case shows: even when contracts are expressly not supposed to contain trade secrets, OOH corporations enforce confidentiality through the courts. Democratic control over the monetization of public infrastructure is structurally circumvented. The pattern — secret financial terms, renewals without tender — can be found in Berlin, Hamburg, Frankfurt, and other German cities.

pol-015.zusammenfassung: A W&V (Werben & Verkaufen, a German advertising industry trade publication) investigation (2017) found: Ströer DSM held outdoor advertising rights in Frankfurt at a fixed lease rate of only €409,000 annually plus revenue sharing — a total of approximately €2.6 million per year for the city. By comparison: Hamburg had re-tendered its OOH rights in 2007 and has since received approximately €34 million per year. Frankfurt was thus receiving, by calculation, **1/13 of the Hamburg market price** for comparable-sized public space.
pol-015.kernbefund: The disparity — €2.6 million vs. €34 million for comparable municipal advertising rights — demonstrates how strongly municipal revenues depend on negotiating power and transparency during the award process. Frankfurt was contractually obligated to re-tender by January 1, 2018. The study implies that without this comparative pressure, many German cities are permanently ceding public space to OOH corporations at far below market value — without democratic oversight of the foregone value.
pol-015.relevanz: This example illustrates the systemic pattern: OOH corporations secure fixed prices far below market value through long-term initial contracts. When contracts expire after 10–20 years, political and institutional dependencies have built up that make a market-rate re-award difficult. The foregone public value — in Frankfurt's case potentially several hundred million euros over a 15-year contract term — is not transparently reported.

priv-001.zusammenfassung: Modern digital advertising screens (DOOH) are increasingly equipped with cameras and sensors that capture biometric data and movement profiles of passers-by in order to deliver targeted advertising ("programmatic") to specific audience segments.
priv-001.kernbefund: Investigations by NGOs show that companies use technologies for Automated Facial Detection (AFD) as well as Wi-Fi sniffing to analyze the age, gender, mood, and dwell time of individuals in front of screens. This occurs in public space, usually without the active consent (opt-in) of those affected, raising serious data protection and ethical concerns.
priv-001.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is evolving from a passive broadcast medium into a proactive surveillance infrastructure in public space. Citizens can barely escape this tracking (opt-out illusion), since they must move through public space.

priv-002.zusammenfassung: The linking of physical advertising locations with digital identity markers enables seamless tracking of citizens in public space.
priv-002.kernbefund: Modern DOOH kiosks (Digital-Out-of-Home) frequently use Wi-Fi and Bluetooth sensors to passively capture the unique MAC addresses or mobile advertising IDs of passers-by. This data is cross-referenced with location data from apps and third-party providers to measure the so-called "path-to-purchase": tracking whether a person who passed a poster later enters the advertised store or searches for the product online. NGOs such as Big Brother Watch criticize that this cross-referencing occurs without the informed consent of citizens and transforms public space into a private surveillance network.
priv-002.relevanz: DOOH is no longer merely an advertisement, but an active sensor in surveillance capitalism. Anonymity in urban space is being systematically abolished through the technological upgrading of advertising infrastructure.

priv-003.zusammenfassung: The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) has clarified that capturing personal characteristics (age, gender, emotions) through camera systems in public advertising installations without valid consent is unlawful. The programmatic DOOH business model, which is based on audience measurement, is therefore structurally incompatible with the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation, known in German as DSGVO — Datenschutz-Grundverordnung).
priv-003.kernbefund: DOOH screens use camera systems for the anonymized counting and classification of passers-by (Anonymized Video Analytics / AVA). The EDPB establishes: even when no biometric templates are stored, the processing of facial and bodily characteristics for audience analysis constitutes processing of personal data pursuant to Art. 4 GDPR. In public space, obtaining valid, informed consent from all those affected is practically impossible.
priv-003.relevanz: Programmatic DOOH booking platforms (e.g., Broadsign, Vistar Media, The Trade Desk) sell "Audience Targeting" for outdoor advertising. This de facto requires that passers-by be analyzed for their demographic characteristics. Companies that book programmatic DOOH expose themselves to considerable GDPR liability risk — particularly following recent million-euro fines from EU data protection authorities.

priv-004.zusammenfassung: Clear Channel Outdoor Americas launched the program "RADAR" in 2016: anonymized location data from mobile phones (via partners such as AT&T, Placed, PlaceIQ) are linked with the reach of Clear Channel billboards in order to analyze the movement patterns of passers-by. US Senator Charles Schumer publicly described the system as "spy billboards." Senator Al Franken formally requested written information on consent mechanisms, data sharing, and security measures. RADAR was subsequently also rolled out in Europe (UK, Spain, Sweden).
priv-004.kernbefund: RADAR uses mobile phone location data to create behavioral patterns and movement profiles of people in public space — without their knowledge and without direct consent. Privacy advocates criticized: the claim of "anonymization" is unverifiable. In Europe, RADAR was adapted for GDPR compliance; the fundamental problem — commercial surveillance of public spaces without active consent — remains structurally unchanged. DOOH displays effectively function as data points in a private surveillance network.
priv-004.relevanz: Clear Channel is one of the three largest OOH corporations worldwide with an extensive European presence. RADAR demonstrates: DOOH is not merely an advertising medium, but an instrument for mass surveillance of public space. Its use as surveillance infrastructure occurs without democratic decision-making — through long-term municipal exclusive contracts, this infrastructure is removed from democratic access.

psych-001.zusammenfassung: Media content — particularly advertising — promotes unrealistic body ideals in children and adolescents. The study documents the causal link between media exposure and the development of eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa.
psych-001.kernbefund: Body dissatisfaction in children and adolescents is directly associated with media consumption and leads to reduced quality of life, deteriorated mood, and unhealthy eating habits. Advertising that portrays unrealistic ideals of thinness is a primary trigger.
psych-001.relevanz: Advertising in public space is unavoidable: children and adolescents are exposed to it daily on their way to school, on public transport, and in shopping zones, with no possibility of opting out. Unlike television or online advertising, outdoor advertising cannot be clicked away or switched off.

psych-002.zusammenfassung: Self-objectification through advertising exposure is linked to body shame, depression, anxiety, and eating disorders. The study analyzes the psychological mechanisms through which advertising content damages the self-image of young people.
psych-002.kernbefund: Exposure to beauty and diet content from advertising accelerates the development of eating disorders. A report by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (2023) found that algorithmically delivered content worsened body image anxiety in 70% of adolescents. Outdoor advertising permanently transports the same images into public space.
psych-002.relevanz: Beauty advertising on billboards and digital screens in public space displays persistent, idealized images to which young people are exposed daily on their routes — with no control over frequency or content.

psych-003.zusammenfassung: Advertising tactics designed to compel attention cause consumers to perceive manipulative intent — thereby reducing advertising effectiveness, brand attitude, and purchase intent. Yet studies show that even recognized manipulation still influences purchasing behavior.
psych-003.kernbefund: When advertising is perceived as manipulative, attitudes toward the advertisement, attitudes toward the brand, and purchase intent all decline significantly. This demonstrates that outdoor advertising is deliberately designed to compel attention — and in doing so violates the cognitive autonomy of passers-by.
psych-003.relevanz: Outdoor advertising deliberately employs stimuli that involuntarily capture attention: garish colors, motion (on digital screens), provocative imagery. In public space, there is no way to circumvent this manipulation.

psych-004.zusammenfassung: Neuroscientific research confirms that subliminal messages can influence decisions under certain conditions — particularly when they align with existing needs or desires. These effects are demonstrable over the long term.
psych-004.kernbefund: Subliminal messages can steer decisions in a particular direction without the affected person noticing. Advertising deliberately exploits these mechanisms: brief image sequences, subliminal messages, and emotional conditioning in outdoor advertising influence behavior below the threshold of conscious perception.
psych-004.relevanz: Digital advertising billboards with changing imagery, brief animations, and emotional visual language use the same mechanisms. Unlike online advertising, these influences in public space cannot be blocked or avoided.

psych-005.zusammenfassung: Empirical study examining the influence of subliminal advertising on purchasing behavior. Non-marketing experts and young consumers are particularly susceptible to unconscious influence through advertising messages.
psych-005.kernbefund: Subliminal advertising measurably influences purchasing behavior, especially among groups without media literacy training. Children and adolescents, as well as individuals without marketing knowledge, are most severely affected.
psych-005.relevanz: Outdoor advertising in public space is directed at the entire population — including the most vulnerable groups (children, people without media literacy). There are no warning systems or protective mechanisms whatsoever.

psych-006.zusammenfassung: Field studies on outdoor advertising show that creativity in advertising visuals is deliberately deployed to hijack involuntary attention and create brand memory through context-dependent memory mechanisms.
psych-006.kernbefund: Outdoor advertising deliberately exploits the orienting response mechanism (unconscious attentional orientation toward novel stimuli), context-dependent memory formation, and cognitive fluency. Creative advertising thereby overcomes a cognitive "attention threshold" — meaning it is designed so as to compel involuntary attention.
psych-006.relevanz: Advertising professionals explicitly design outdoor advertising so that it involuntarily draws the gaze of passers-by — that is its stated purpose. This deliberate manipulation of involuntary cognition in public space occurs without the consent of those affected.

psych-007.zusammenfassung: The psychology behind digital screens (DOOH) is based on the exploitation of evolutionary reflexes. Unlike static posters, changing or moving images compel the human brain to look.
psych-007.kernbefund: The so-called orienting response (Orientierungsreflex) is an involuntary neurological mechanism that compels people to pay attention to sudden changes in their peripheral visual field (such as changes in light or motion on a screen), since this is evolutionarily associated with danger. DOOH installations deliberately exploit this reflex to "steal" attention. One cannot decide not to look.
psych-007.relevanz: Digital advertising billboards are psychologically far more aggressive than traditional OOH (out-of-home) posters. They represent a permanent cognitive stressor in public space, as they keep the brain in a constant state of alertness.

psych-008.zusammenfassung: Modern advertising screens are equipped with sensors that scan the audience in real time in order to psychologically optimize advertising messages.
psych-008.kernbefund: An increasing number of DOOH installations integrate camera systems that capture the faces of passers-by using "Anonymized Video Analytics" (AVA). The technology analyzes in fractions of a second the age, gender, dwell time, and in some cases even the emotional reaction (mood) to the displayed advertising. Although the industry claims not to store images, the analysis occurs without the knowledge or consent of passers-by. This "eye tracking" in public space is used to perfect the effectiveness of manipulation techniques and to systematically undermine the cognitive defenses of citizens.
psych-008.relevanz: Public space is becoming a laboratory for the advertising industry. Passers-by are involuntarily turned into test subjects in a mass-psychological experiment in which every reaction is biometrically recorded and commercially exploited.

psych-009.zusammenfassung: Peer-reviewed analysis of the long-term consequences of advertising exposure on children: advertising instills materialistic values that are in direct conflict with prosocial behavior, intrinsic motivation, and psychological resilience.
psych-009.kernbefund: Children who are intensively exposed to advertising demonstrably develop stronger materialistic attitudes — the equation of possessions with happiness, status, and identity. This correlates with lower self-esteem, increased dissatisfaction, and reduced life satisfaction in adulthood. Outdoor advertising in public space is particularly effective at producing this conditioning, as it represents a permanent, non-consent-based exposure.
psych-009.relevanz: Unlike TV advertising, OOH/DOOH in public space cannot be switched off — children on their way to school, while playing, or in the city cannot escape this exposure. The psychological conditioning through materialistic messages thus takes place without parental oversight or control.

reg-001.zusammenfassung: Since 2024, a popular initiative (Hamburg Werbefrei — Hamburg Ad-Free) has been underway in Hamburg to restrict outdoor advertising, in particular digital advertising screens. The Hamburg Constitutional Court (Hamburgisches Verfassungsgericht) declared the initiative legally admissible in September 2024.
reg-001.kernbefund: The Hamburg Constitutional Court ruled that the initiative "Hamburg Werbefrei" (Hamburg Ad-Free) is constitutionally permissible. Around 400 activists collected over 50,000 signatures in 3 weeks (target: 80,000 = 5% of eligible voters, required for a binding referendum — Volksentscheid). The initiative calls for a ban on digital advertising screens and a reduction in poster advertising on grounds of environmental, public health, and urban landscape protection.
