reg-001.relevanz: The Hamburg initiative demonstrates that there is broad public support for restrictions on outdoor advertising. When a major German city holds a democratic vote on advertising bans, it sends a powerful signal that society recognises the harms caused by outdoor advertising.

reg-002.zusammenfassung: Germany was the last EU member state to ban outdoor tobacco advertising. The ban was introduced in stages: tobacco products from January 2022, heated tobacco products from January 2023, and e-cigarettes from January 2024.
reg-002.kernbefund: The tobacco industry spent approximately 100 million euros per year on street and cinema advertising in Germany. For decades Germany was a special case within the EU: while other member states had long since banned outdoor tobacco advertising, Germany's politically influential tobacco industry blocked the prohibition. The ban only came following significant public and EU pressure.
reg-002.relevanz: This example illustrates how the advertising industry can delay legislative safeguards for decades, even when the harm — tobacco advertising leading to youth smoking — has long been scientifically established. It sets a precedent for other harmful advertising in public spaces.

reg-003.zusammenfassung: São Paulo introduced the "Lei Cidade Limpa" (Clean City Law) in 2007 — the most comprehensive outdoor advertising ban in the world. 15,000 billboards were removed, digital screens banned, advertising on buses prohibited, and 300,000 non-compliant business signs taken down.
reg-003.kernbefund: A survey in 2011 (4 years after the ban) showed that 70% of São Paulo's 11 million residents regarded the ban positively. Unexpected consequences: the ban revealed historic architecture that had previously been obscured by advertising, and it stimulated street art. Clear Channel challenged the law in court — and lost.
reg-003.relevanz: São Paulo is proof that life without outdoor advertising in public spaces is possible — and is welcomed by the majority of the population. It refutes the advertising industry's argument that outdoor advertising is an indispensable part of city life.

reg-004.zusammenfassung: Grenoble (France) became the first European city to introduce a comprehensive outdoor advertising ban in its urban area in 2015. Mayor Éric Piolle (Greens) terminated the city's billboard contract and had 326 advertising panels (including 64 large billboards) removed.
reg-004.kernbefund: 2,051 square metres of advertising space were eliminated. As a replacement: 300+ new community notice boards (Bürgertafeln) for non-profit announcements, trees, and open spaces for local cultural groups. Financial loss: 600,000 euros per year in advertising revenue. The model demonstrates that cities can forgo advertising revenue and reclaim public space.
reg-004.relevanz: Grenoble proves that it is politically and financially feasible to eliminate outdoor advertising in a European city. The city is now a reference case for urban ad-free movements worldwide.

reg-005.zusammenfassung: Analysis by the European consumer organisation BEUC (Bureau Européen des Unions de Consommateurs) of the EU Pledge — the food industry's voluntary commitment not to advertise unhealthy products to children. Conclusion: total failure of self-regulation.
reg-005.kernbefund: 21 companies responsible for over 80% of European food advertising expenditure have signed up to the EU Pledge. Nevertheless, 85% of the products these companies market to children would be prohibited from advertising under WHO nutritional criteria. Voluntary self-regulatory commitments are ineffective.
reg-005.relevanz: Outdoor advertising in Germany and the EU is also governed primarily by self-regulation (Deutscher Werberat — German Advertising Standards Council). This example demonstrates systemically that voluntary industry codes do not protect children. Statutory prohibitions are necessary.

reg-006.zusammenfassung: Academic analysis of the structural weaknesses of German advertising self-regulation (Deutscher Werberat — German Advertising Standards Council). Documents structural deficiencies that prevent effective consumer protection.
reg-006.kernbefund: The Deutscher Werberat (German Advertising Standards Council) has no consumer representation on its board — only a liaison committee. It can demand voluntary compliance but has no binding enforcement powers. Advertising practices can continue unimpeded while proceedings are in progress. In 2023 the Council issued only 8 formal reprimands (Rügen) despite thousands of advertisements in circulation.
reg-006.relevanz: Outdoor advertising in Germany is in practice subject to no effective substantive regulation. The Werberat is the principal protective instrument — and it does not protect. This leaves harmful advertising in public spaces structurally unregulated.

reg-007.zusammenfassung: In 2021, §41a was inserted into the Bundesnaturschutzgesetz (BNatSchG — Federal Nature Conservation Act), providing for protection against light emissions. The provision is not yet in force — it requires an implementing ordinance (Durchführungsverordnung) announced for 2027 as part of the national biodiversity strategy.
reg-007.kernbefund: The German legislature has officially recognised light pollution as a nature conservation problem and incorporated it into the Federal Nature Conservation Act. Illuminated advertising panels and digital DOOH screens in Germany are in urban areas almost twice as numerous as street lamps, and contribute substantially to light pollution.
reg-007.relevanz: If §41a BNatSchG comes into force in 2027, it could for the first time provide a statutory basis for regulating advertising illumination as a source of light emissions. At present, specific statutory rules for outdoor advertising illumination in Germany are lacking.

reg-008.zusammenfassung: In several large cities in North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW) — particularly Cologne (Köln), the home city of Ströer, and Münster — civil society initiatives have formed that are calling for a ban or strong restrictions on commercial outdoor advertising.
reg-008.kernbefund: These initiatives aim to amend local building regulations (Bauordnung) so that digital advertising installations (DOOH) and alternating illuminated signs in public spaces are prohibited. They argue on grounds of visual noise (visueller Lärm), unnecessary energy consumption during the climate crisis, and the commercialisation of cities.
reg-008.relevanz: Resistance to outdoor advertising is coalescing strongly at grassroots level directly within the municipalities where the advertising structures are installed. This reflects the growing discontent of civil society with the privatisation of public space.

reg-009.zusammenfassung: Advertising corporations exploit gaps in municipal building and planning regulations to digitalise public spaces without renewed public participation.
reg-009.kernbefund: In many municipalities, contracts or permits exist for existing "illuminated advertising installations" (e.g. analogue City Light Posters). Outdoor advertisers are increasingly using these existing permits to physically replace the paper poster with a bright DOOH LED screen ("digital upgrade"). Because the physical dimensions of the casing often remain the same, planning authorities frequently — and incorrectly — do not classify this as a new construction, thereby bypassing environmental assessments and objections from local residents.
reg-009.relevanz: The stark differences in light emission and psychological impact between an analogue poster and a digital screen are being ignored through legal technicalities. A rigorous update of building regulations is urgently needed.

reg-010.zusammenfassung: The installation and operation of digital billboards frequently violates local building regulations. Corporations exploit the overloaded capacity of municipal authorities.
reg-010.kernbefund: Investigations in the United Kingdom reveal systematic disregard for conditions and requirements. DOOH installations are often erected entirely without planning permission. Even where conditions exist, contractually agreed brightness limits (luminance) are exceeded, or mandatory night-time switch-offs (e.g. from 23:00 to 06:00) are simply ignored. Advertising corporations often accept fines as a "cost of doing business", since revenue from the illegal advertising airtime is higher, and municipal planning departments are too understaffed to pursue Discontinuance Notices through the courts.
reg-010.relevanz: The industry cannot be effectively controlled. Once the hardware is physically installed, the burden of proof (measuring brightness) and the effort of legal enforcement rests entirely with municipalities and local residents.

reg-011.zusammenfassung: A growing number of municipal and regional governments are using their role as landowners to ban advertising for high-emission products on civic infrastructure.
reg-011.kernbefund: Cities including Edinburgh, Sheffield, Cambridgeshire, and Somerset have introduced legally binding clauses into their advertising policies. These prohibit advertising corporations (such as JCDecaux or Clear Channel) from displaying advertising for flights, fossil-fuel-powered SUVs, and fossil fuels on municipal land (e.g. bus shelters, council-owned hoardings). The municipalities argue that promoting these products is in direct contradiction to their urban climate protection targets ("Net Zero").
reg-011.relevanz: These policy frameworks prove that regulating the *content* of outdoor advertising at the local level is legally feasible and politically supported. They place "high-carbon" products on the same prohibited footing as tobacco or weapons advertising.

reg-012.zusammenfassung: The legal assumption that a complete ban on outdoor advertising constitutes an impermissible interference with economic freedom (Wirtschaftsfreiheit) has been refuted by Switzerland's highest court.
reg-012.kernbefund: The municipality of Vernier (Canton of Geneva) resolved to ban commercial poster advertising throughout its territory in order to protect the visual landscape and reduce visual environmental pollution. Advertising corporations (including APG SGA) challenged the ban through every level of the court system. In 2024, the Swiss Federal Supreme Court (Bundesgericht) issued a final ruling in favour of the municipality: the ban is lawful. The court found that the public interest in an intact local environment and in protecting residents from unsolicited consumer pressure outweighs the purely commercial interests of the advertising industry.
reg-012.relevanz: This ruling is a massive legal precedent for the whole of Europe. It gives cities and municipalities the legal certainty that zero-billboard policies are proportionate and enforceable.

reg-013.zusammenfassung: Bodies of "voluntary self-regulation" (such as the Werberat — Advertising Standards Council — in Germany, or the ASA — Advertising Standards Authority — in the UK) are unable to effectively prevent harmful outdoor advertising.
reg-013.kernbefund: The advertising industry's self-regulatory systems share a structural design flaw: they operate almost exclusively reactively. There is no pre-clearance process for posters. This means that severely harmful or misleading advertising is first displayed and forced upon the public (including children). By the time complaints are submitted, reviewed, and formal reprimands issued, the typical one-to-two-week booking period for the poster has in any case already expired. The harm has already occurred.
reg-013.relevanz: "We comply with the rules of the Werberat" is an industry argument that implies safety but is in practice worthless. To protect citizens, cities must legally enshrine proactive exclusion criteria (such as London's junk food ban) into binding policy.

reg-014.zusammenfassung: A strict ban on outdoor advertising is not an economic disadvantage but a tangible economic competitive advantage — as four US states demonstrate.
reg-014.kernbefund: In the United States, the four states of Hawaii, Maine, Vermont, and Alaska have banned outdoor advertising across their entire territories by law. Contrary to the advertising industry's claim that bans harm local economies, the governments of these states argue the opposite: protecting the landscape ("Scenic Beauty") from visual pollution ("Billboard Blight") is a decisive factor in promoting tourism and quality of life. Preserving an unobstructed landscape is economically more valuable than advertising revenue.
reg-014.relevanz: These substantial legal precedents undermine the industry's "TINA" argument (There Is No Alternative). A complete ban on outdoor advertising is implementable at state level and economically sound.

reg-015.zusammenfassung: The French government has enacted landmark climate and advertising legislation at the national level that directly affects the business models of OOH (out-of-home) and DOOH (digital out-of-home) operators.
reg-015.kernbefund: The "Loi Climat et Résilience" (Climate and Resilience Act), which entered into force in August 2022, bans advertising for fossil fuels (gas, coal, oil) nationwide. Additionally, this law now formally grants mayors and local authorities ("Maires") executive policing powers (Pouvoir de Police — executive enforcement authority) to strictly restrict or completely remove digital and illuminated advertising panels within their municipal area by local decree. Previously, this decision-making authority often resided at uncertain intermediate national-regional levels.
reg-015.relevanz: This is one of the most powerful legislative interventions in the EU. Advertising for climate-damaging products is placed on the same footing as tobacco advertising, and decision-making authority over digital light pollution is formally returned to cities.

reg-016.zusammenfassung: Dutch cities are using their control over public space to actively reduce consumption of climate-damaging products.
reg-016.kernbefund: As the first capital city in the world, Amsterdam passed a law in 2026 prohibiting advertising for meat products and fossil fuels (cars, flights, oil) at municipal advertising sites (bus shelters, railway stations). Haarlem pioneered this movement in 2022. The aim is to support the cities' climate targets by ending the visual normalisation of products with a high carbon footprint. The cities argue that providing public space for the promotion of climate-damaging products is in direct contradiction to the public interest mandate.
reg-016.relevanz: This ban proves that municipalities have the right to filter the *content* of outdoor advertising according to ethical and ecological criteria in order to meet their climate protection commitments.

reg-017.zusammenfassung: French environmental law actively protects rural areas and smaller municipalities from the visual flooding of commercial advertising.
reg-017.kernbefund: As part of a comprehensive reform of advertising law, France enacted legislation in 2010 that has been fully applicable since July 2015: in all municipalities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants (that are not part of a larger metropolitan area), large-format commercial outdoor billboard advertising is fundamentally prohibited. Permitted only are specific directional signs for local cultural activities, regional products, or essential services. Violations expose advertisers to daily fines.
reg-017.relevanz: The law demonstrates that preserving the aesthetic integrity and quality of life in smaller municipalities is a protectable public interest that takes precedence over the commercial exploitation interests of the advertising industry.

reg-018.zusammenfassung: Planning law gives cities the means to limit visual clutter (Clutter) and the associated degradation of quality of life in residential neighbourhoods.
reg-018.kernbefund: In Bristol (UK), the city council has tightened guidelines interpreting the concept of "amenity" (quality of life / livability) in planning law. The aim is to prevent digital advertising screens from being disproportionately concentrated in districts that already have lower environmental quality or in lower-income neighbourhoods. The city argues that an excessive density of DOOH installations degrades the appearance of a neighbourhood, creates light pollution for residents, and violates the right to an ad-free, peaceful public space.
reg-018.relevanz: This is an instrument for enforcing spatial equity (räumliche Gerechtigkeit). It challenges the industry practice of flooding low-income neighbourhoods with cheap advertising while affluent neighbourhoods remain "clean".

reg-019.zusammenfassung: Belgium became the first country in the world in 2023 to completely ban advertising for fossil fuels at the national level — including all outdoor advertising surfaces (OOH/DOOH). The law is regarded as a blueprint for similar regulation at EU level.
reg-019.kernbefund: The Belgian ban covers all media including OOH/DOOH and applies to advertising that promotes the consumption of fossil fuels (petroleum, natural gas, coal). The Belgian competition authority (Belgische Wettbewerbsbehörde) is responsible for enforcement. The law followed a successful lawsuit by NGOs against greenwashing advertising by energy corporations. France had previously restricted fossil fuel advertising with the Loi Climat (2022) — Belgium goes further.
reg-019.relevanz: For DOOH network operators who generate substantial revenue from the energy sector (oil companies, gas initiatives, automotive manufacturers), the Belgian model poses a direct revenue risk if further EU countries follow suit. Germany is discussing similar regulations in the context of the Klimaschutzgesetz (Federal Climate Protection Act).

reg-020.zusammenfassung: A Tagesspiegel interview with the JCDecaux CEO: the managing director of the world's largest outdoor advertising company openly admits that the corporation deliberately cultivates networks with political decision-makers in cities in order to secure advertising rights contracts. This is the structural foundation of the "street furniture" (Stadtmöbel) business model.
reg-020.kernbefund: JCDecaux's business model is explicitly based on building relationships with political decision-makers in municipalities who decide on the allocation of advertising rights. The CEO stated: *"We know how to deal with decision-makers."* JCDecaux holds a 15-year exclusive contract in Cologne (Köln) for 1,550 passenger shelters and 350 city information systems. In Berlin, JCDecaux/Wall held the dominant street furniture contract for decades. Karlsruhe also renewed its advertising rights contracts with Wall/JCDecaux.
reg-020.relevanz: The "street furniture" (Stadtmöbel) model is not a service offering — it is a political lobbying strategy: municipalities receive infrastructure (bus shelters, clocks, public toilets) and in return grant exclusive advertising rights for 10–20 years, giving the corporation de facto control over public space. No city council can pass advertising bans during that period without risking contractual penalties.

reg-021.zusammenfassung: The Hague (Den Haag, Netherlands, population 500,000) became — as of 1 January 2025 — the first city in the world with a statutory ban on OOH advertising for fossil fuel products: specifically petrol/diesel vehicles, flights, and cruises. The ban applies to all billboards and bus shelters in public space. Other EU cities are following.
reg-021.kernbefund: The Den Haag ban is **a direct OOH/DOOH prohibition** — it explicitly covers billboards and passenger shelters in public space. The city thus heeds the call of UN Secretary-General António Guterres, who demanded a global ban on advertising for fossil fuels. In response, the Dutch travel association ANVR announced legal action. Further cities that are discussing or have enacted similar bans include: Amsterdam, Edinburgh, Sydney, Zwolle, Tilburg, and Graz (Austria). Belgium enacted a national fossil fuel advertising ban (all media) in 2023.
reg-021.relevanz: The Hague demonstrates that OOH/DOOH advertising for specific product categories can be legally banned — despite existing advertising rights contracts with corporations. The model will spread across the EU. For DOOH investors: two of the most lucrative advertising categories (automotive and aviation) are already banned in The Hague — with a signal effect for other EU markets, including Germany.

reg-022.zusammenfassung: The Hamburg Regional Court (Landgericht Hamburg) banned Shell Deutschland by judgment on 9 August 2024 from advertising with the promise "CO2-neutral driving for 1.1 cents per litre." The Deutsche Umwelthilfe (German Environmental Aid, a German environmental NGO) had filed suit in 2022 after Shell failed to cease the practice despite a formal warning (Abmahnung). The court ruled: the advertising was "highly misleading for consumers."
reg-022.kernbefund: Shell promised CO2 neutrality in its petrol station and OOH advertising through offset projects (forest protection in Peru and Indonesia). The court (case no. 315 O 108/22) found: (1) the advertising was not transparent about the offset method; (2) forest protection projects cannot reliably offset CO2 persistence over centuries — forests can release stored CO2 within years or decades. The Deutsche Umwelthilfe had established that across 6 major energy corporations, **81% of Shell's advertisements constituted greenwashing**.
reg-022.relevanz: The ruling applies directly to OOH advertising: Shell petrol station advertising and outdoor campaigns were part of the impugned advertising measures. The ruling sets a precedent for Germany: vague "climate neutrality" promises in OOH campaigns are legally challengeable. DOOH network operators that carry greenwashing campaigns from energy corporations expose themselves — and their clients — to legal risks.

reg-023.zusammenfassung: The European Commission opened a formal state aid (Staatsbeihilfe) investigation in 2015 into two contracts between the City of Brussels and JCDecaux. Result in 2019: JCDecaux had continued operating advertising panels ("phantom billboards") after the contracts expired — without paying rent or taxes. This constitutes illegal state aid incompatible with the EU internal market. The EU General Court (Gericht der Europäischen Union, EuG) dismissed JCDecaux's appeal.
reg-023.kernbefund: JCDecaux used municipal infrastructure in Brussels beyond the contractually agreed period without paying any consideration. Competitors had to pay regular market prices for comparable advertising rights. The European Commission classified this as an impermissible competitive advantage. The EU General Court (case no. T-642/19) upheld the Commission decision and dismissed JCDecaux's action in full. Competitor Clear Channel Belgium had filed the original complaint.
reg-023.relevanz: This case documents the structural pattern in the OOH market: advertising corporations secure public spaces on preferential terms and control over infrastructure that properly belongs to the general public, through opaque contract arrangements. The EU state aid procedure provides the highest conceivable institutional evidence for the thesis that JCDecaux systematically exploits municipal institutions for its own benefit. Investors and municipalities in the EU are directly exposed to this risk.

reg-024.zusammenfassung: The Swiss Federal Supreme Court (Bundesgericht) confirmed in 2024 that the municipality of Vernier (38,000 inhabitants, Canton of Geneva) may ban all commercial advertising panels in public space — including on private land. The ban serves to combat "visual pollution" and grants citizens the right to withdraw from unwanted advertising. More than three quarters of the 172 advertising panels have been removed. Zurich (Zürich) and Berne (Bern) have announced similar bans. OOH companies in Switzerland reportedly face an "existential threat."
reg-024.kernbefund: The Federal Supreme Court did not classify the complete advertising ban as an anti-competitive intervention but as a legitimate municipal measure against "visual environmental pollution" (visuelle Umweltverschmutzung). In Switzerland it is now legally recognised: outdoor advertising in public space is a form of environmental pollution against which citizens have a right to protection. The precedent ruling applies to all Swiss municipalities. Zurich in particular targets digital screens due to their energy consumption and light pollution.
reg-024.relevanz: The Federal Supreme Court ruling is the strongest judicial confirmation worldwide that complete OOH bans are legally sustainable. The "domino effect" in Switzerland — Vernier → Zurich → Berne — shows that a single precedent ruling can trigger an avalanche. For DOOH investors counting on long-term revenue from public locations, the Swiss model is a direct precursor to European legal developments.

reg-025.zusammenfassung: Amsterdam passed a law in January 2026 (by 27:17 council votes) — the first statutory ban by a capital city on OOH advertising for fossil fuels, meat, flights, petrol/diesel vehicles, and gas heating — covering all public surfaces including trams, trains, buses, and digital screens. In force from 1 May 2026. A second phase bans, from April 2028, corporate image advertising by high-emission companies as well. The city council withstood intensive lobbying pressure from industry and the national government.
reg-025.kernbefund: Amsterdam goes beyond The Hague (fossil fuels only) by including meat and flights for the first time. The vote was passed despite a final lobbying offensive. The ban covers all DOOH networks in public space. The 2028 second phase explicitly targets "Corporate Image Advertising" by companies with high CO₂ emissions — a precedent for corporate brand communications. The city council described lobbying by industry and government as inappropriate interference in democratic decision-making processes.
reg-025.relevanz: Amsterdam is the first EU capital city with such a ban. Together with The Hague (2025), Belgium (2023), France (2022), and now Amsterdam (2026), a tightening regulatory web is forming across the EU. Two of the most valuable DOOH categories — automotive and food — are banned in Amsterdam. DOOH investments in EU capital cities carry a structural and accelerating regulatory risk that threatens the profitability of existing contracts.

reg-026.zusammenfassung: EU Directive 2024/825 ("Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition"), adopted on 27 March 2024, bans generic environmental claims in advertising without specific evidence on the same medium. Banned from September 2026 (national transposition required by March 2026): statements such as "CO2-neutral", "climate-friendly", "energy-efficient", "green", "biodegradable" without quantified substantiation. Also banned: climate neutrality claims based solely on CO₂ offset projects.
reg-026.kernbefund: The Directive applies to all advertising formats — including OOH and DOOH. Since billboards offer physically limited space, generic greenwashing claims on DOOH screens will in practice become impossible: a "CO2-neutral" claim on a digital display without detailed supporting evidence on the same medium will be EU-unlawful from 2026. The associated Green Claims Directive (more detailed regulation) was withdrawn by the Commission in 2025 — but Directive 2024/825 remains in force.
reg-026.relevanz: DOOH networks in Germany and the EU generate substantial revenue from campaigns by energy companies, automotive manufacturers, and airlines carrying greenwashing messages. From September 2026, these campaigns in their current form will be EU-unlawful. DOOH operators bear co-responsibility for disseminating misleading advertising on their infrastructure — the Hamburg Regional Court (Landgericht Hamburg) confirmed this in 2024 in the Shell case (reg-022).

res-001.zusammenfassung: Adfree Cities UK measured the electricity consumption of various types of digital out-of-home advertising displays and compared them with household electricity usage.
res-001.kernbefund: A large digital advertising display (6.4 m × 3.1 m) consumes **41,627 kWh per year** — equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of 11 British households. A medium-sized display (1.2 m × 1.8 m, "Six Sheet") consumes 11,501 kWh/year (3 households). A double-sided unit in a city center consumes as much as 4 households. At night (10 pm–6 am), one large display consumes as much as 8.5 households during the same period.
res-001.relevanz: Every digital billboard in public space consumes energy around the clock — exclusively for commercial purposes. This energy consumption provides no social benefit and directly competes with the goals of the energy transition (Energiewende).

res-002.zusammenfassung: A city-wide measurement of the electricity consumption of digital advertising screens in Leeds (UK) by Adfree Cities. Compared with the electricity consumption of the city's population.
res-002.kernbefund: The digital advertising screens in Leeds consume a total of **4.1 GWh per year** — enough to power 3,300 residents. This is the measured electricity consumption solely for commercial out-of-home advertising in a medium-sized British city.
res-002.relevanz: This figure makes the cumulative costs of outdoor advertising tangible at a city scale: the advertising in a single city consumes as much electricity as a medium-sized town. Scaled up across all cities in Germany or Europe, the result is a massive and avoidable energy consumption.

res-003.zusammenfassung: During the energy crisis of 2022 (triggered by Russia's halt of gas supplies), Germany, together with Austria, Spain and France, mandated that digital advertising screens be switched off between 10 pm and 6 am. Berlin's Kurfürstendamm (a major commercial boulevard) and other high-visibility advertising sites went dark at night.
res-003.kernbefund: During the 2022 energy crisis, digital advertising displays in several EU countries were classified as non-essential energy consumers and shut down at night. This constitutes an explicit government acknowledgement that outdoor advertising ranks below essential energy consumers.
res-003.relevanz: When the state shuts down advertising screens first in a crisis, it implicitly confirms: outdoor advertising is not a public benefit, but a luxury consumption of resources that is immediately dispensable when supply is constrained.

res-004.zusammenfassung: Data from the EU-funded ECOBOARD project (CORDIS) and EnKad Sciences on the volume of waste generated by advertising banners and billboards.
res-004.kernbefund: In the United States alone, **600,000 tonnes of PVC advertising banner waste** are disposed of annually. In the Brussels region, 10,000 billboards generate **68,000 m² (approx. 680 tonnes) of vinyl waste** per year. Across Europe, more than **6 million m² of poster paper** is discarded — not recycled — **every 2 weeks**, containing environmentally harmful printing inks and toxic adhesives.
res-004.relevanz: Advertising banners consist of 33% PVC resin, 36% calcium carbonate, 18% polyester fiber, and 9% plasticizers (phthalates). This material requires over **1,000 years to decompose** in landfills. Outdoor advertising is one of the largest sources of short-lived PVC plastic waste in public space.

res-005.zusammenfassung: Greenpeace analysis of the toxicity of PVC (polyvinyl chloride) across its entire lifecycle. PVC is the material used in the vast majority of all outdoor advertising banners and poster backings.
res-005.kernbefund: PVC causes environmental and health damage at every stage: **Production** (PVC consumes 30–40% of all industrially produced chlorine; generates dioxins), **Use** (plasticizers/phthalates leach out and damage the hormonal system, reproduction, and respiratory tract), and **Disposal** (release of dioxins during incineration; 1,000+ years decomposition time in landfills). Phthalates from PVC are detected in waterways, air, and human tissue.
res-005.relevanz: Outdoor advertising banners are among the shortest-lived PVC products in existence: they are replaced every 4 weeks — for each new advertising campaign. The entire lifecycle of this toxic material serves exclusively the commercial purpose of capturing attention.

res-006.zusammenfassung: Scientific analysis of the chemical ingredients in printing inks used for large-format printing (as used for outdoor advertising and billboards). Printing inks are an often-overlooked component of the environmental costs of outdoor advertising.
res-006.kernbefund: Printing inks used for advertising contain as their primary solvents **toluene (approx. 70% of all emitted chemicals)**, as well as methyl ethyl ketone, xylene, and 1,1,1-trichloroethane — all volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and hazardous air pollutants (HAPs). Additionally: **cadmium, lead** (heavy metals), **bisphenol A (BPA)** (an endocrine disruptor), and synthetic antioxidants.
res-006.relevanz: Every advertising print releases these chemicals into the air — in printing facilities and through off-gassing from posters in public space. The production of advertising materials is an industrial chemical source that is restarted with every campaign change.

res-007.zusammenfassung: A peer-reviewed study assessing the external costs of outdoor advertising in Warsaw (Poland) by measuring residents' willingness to pay for a reduction in advertising.
res-007.kernbefund:
Warsaw residents were willing to pay:
- **€1.7–4.1 million/year** for a reduction in freestanding advertising structures
- **€5.5–9.3 million/year** for a reduction in building-mounted advertising
- An average of **€15–23 per person per year** for advertising reduction

These figures quantify the external costs of outdoor advertising that are currently borne entirely by the public and not compensated by the advertising industry.
res-007.relevanz: The study is the first to quantify the economic harm that outdoor advertising inflicts on urban residents — in the form of uncompensated external costs. Scaled up to major German cities, this represents a substantial societal cost factor.

res-008.zusammenfassung: An economic analysis of the attention economy as an external cost factor. Examines whether a Pigouvian tax on attention capture by advertising is justified.
res-008.kernbefund: According to APA (American Psychological Association) research, attention interruptions from advertising and other distractions destroy up to **40% of productive working time**. Multitasking and forced attention-switching deplete neural glucose reserves disproportionately. The authors propose a Pigouvian tax on attention capture — analogous to environmental taxes — because the cognitive costs are fully externalized: advertisers profit while those affected bear the costs.
res-008.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is designed to force involuntary attention (cf. psych-006). The associated cognitive costs are entirely externalized and borne by passersby without consent and without compensation.

res-010.zusammenfassung: Technical lifecycle analysis of digital LED billboards compared with traditional static billboards. Assesses manufacturing and operational emissions.
res-010.kernbefund: The **manufacture of a digital billboard** generates a **3.5 times larger CO₂ footprint** than the manufacture of a traditional static billboard. LED displays over 10 years can, however, save 18 tonnes of CO₂ in operation compared with LCD screens. The manufacturing phase alone means: every new digital billboard represents a substantial CO₂ investment that takes years to amortize.
res-010.relevanz: The global DOOH market is growing at 12% per year — new screens are being installed en masse. Every installation generates 3.5 times the manufacturing CO₂ footprint of a traditional billboard, before a single advertisement has been shown.

res-011.zusammenfassung: Despite the shift to LED technology, the absolute energy consumption of digital billboards (DOOH) remains immensely high, as they illuminate continuously around the clock, require cooling, and emit extremely high brightness.
res-011.kernbefund: Research confirms that a typical double-sided digital advertising screen at a bus stop consumes approximately 11,000 to 14,000 kWh of electricity per year. This is equivalent to the electricity consumption of three to four average households. This massive consumption of resources takes place in the midst of a global energy and climate crisis.
res-011.relevanz: DOOH is in direct contradiction to urban and national energy-saving targets. The "Net Zero" strategies promoted by the industry often only offset, but do not reduce, the exorbitant direct electricity consumption of the hardware.

safety-001.zusammenfassung: A comprehensive collection of studies by Scenic America shows that digital billboards (DOOH) divert drivers' gaze from the road significantly longer than static signs.
safety-001.kernbefund: A glance away from the road lasting more than two seconds — which is frequently triggered by changing or animated digital content — dramatically increases the risk of an accident. Studies conducted in the United States (including in Alabama and Florida) document elevated crash rates in the immediate vicinity of such installations.
safety-001.relevanz: DOOH installations are not merely visual pollution, but a concrete risk to public road safety. The profit interests of the advertising industry are in direct conflict with protecting road users.

safety-002.zusammenfassung: The advertising industry frequently cites studies (such as the 2013 FHWA study) to claim that digital billboards are traffic-safe. Independent reviews, however, reveal serious methodological flaws in these industry-supported investigations.
safety-002.kernbefund: Independent traffic safety experts (such as Jerry Wachtel) demonstrate that exculpatory studies often suffer from excessively small sample sizes, inadequate measuring instruments, and flawed experimental designs. Independent data consistently shows an elevated risk of cognitive and visual distraction.
safety-002.relevanz: The safety of DOOH advertising is being systematically downplayed through targeted lobbying and potentially flawed government studies.

safety-003.zusammenfassung: A detailed field study by the Swedish Transport Administration (Trafikverket) demonstrated that digital billboards significantly distract drivers. As a direct consequence, the Swedish government ordered the removal of the billboards.
safety-003.kernbefund: The study found that drivers averted their gaze from the road significantly longer at DOOH installations (often exceeding 2 seconds) compared with static signs. Since gaze diversions exceeding 2 seconds are considered highly dangerous, the government decided that the economic interests of operators must be subordinated to the protection of traffic safety. The pilot program for approving such billboards was subsequently terminated.
safety-003.relevanz: Government studies free from industry influence reach clear, negative conclusions regarding the traffic safety of DOOH installations and can lead to rigorous bans.

safety-004.zusammenfassung: The extreme luminance of digital billboards can impede the perception of critical traffic signals and emergency vehicles.
safety-004.kernbefund: It is well established in the psychology of visual perception that stronger light stimuli can mask weaker ones. High-power LED screens positioned in the line of sight to traffic signals or road signs can drastically reduce their signal effectiveness, particularly at night or in poor weather conditions (rain, fog). Furthermore, the enormous brightness and color dynamics of DOOH installations can cause the flashing warning lights of approaching emergency vehicles (blue light) to be lost in the visual noise of the surroundings, or to be perceived too late — dangerously extending the reaction time of road users.
safety-004.relevanz: Outdoor advertising poses a safety risk when it competes with official safety infrastructure for visual dominance. Prioritizing advertising messages can, in critical situations, endanger human lives.

safety-005.zusammenfassung: A peer-reviewed investigation of distraction effects on pedestrians in urban environments. Digital and animated outdoor advertising significantly increases visual distraction and raises the risk of accidents at intersections and crossings.
safety-005.kernbefund: Pedestrians and cyclists exposed to visually distracting stimuli (screens, moving image changes) show measurably delayed reaction times at road crossings, more frequent crossing without visual contact with traffic, and increased error rates in situation assessment. Digital advertising formats with high light intensity and moving images (DOOH) are more effective than static advertising in their distracting effect.
safety-005.relevanz: Unlike driver distraction from DOOH (which is widely documented), pedestrian and cyclist distraction has so far barely been addressed in DOOH regulation. In cities with high pedestrian and cycling density (Berlin, Hamburg, Amsterdam), risk exposure from DOOH screens at intersections is particularly relevant.

safety-006.zusammenfassung: The Swedish Transport Administration (Trafikverket) had twelve digital billboards installed on a trial basis on a three-lane urban motorway section in Stockholm. An instrumented vehicle study with 41 drivers using eye-tracking documented that: digital billboards were fixated significantly longer than other road signs on the same section. Gaze-diversion times frequently exceeded the critical 2-second threshold (beyond which distraction is considered dangerous). Result: Trafikverket decided to remove the digital billboards from the motorway section. The study was published in Accident Analysis & Prevention.
safety-006.kernbefund: The study design — real road, instrumented vehicle, eye-tracking — is methodologically stronger than simulator studies. The measurements showed "considerably longer dwell time, greater fixation count, and longer maximum fixation duration" for DOOH billboards compared with static signs. This is the rare case in which an authority acted directly following its own study: the digital billboards were removed on the basis of the research findings. The result refutes the industry's claim that DOOH is safe for traffic.
safety-006.relevanz: The Swedish study is one of the methodologically strongest pieces of evidence for the traffic hazard posed by DOOH on high-speed roads — and the most direct evidence of a regulatory consequence: not merely a recommendation, but a decision to remove the installations. Cities and road authorities that grant DOOH concessions for sites on high-speed roads do so contrary to the existing body of research.

safety-007.zusammenfassung: A government-funded US study analyzed 18 digital billboard locations on US highways. Sites in Florida showed **25% higher crash rates** and sites in Alabama showed **29% higher crash rates** — compared with control sites on the same road sections without digital billboards. The study was funded by the US Department of Transportation (DOT) and conducted at the Georgia Institute of Technology.
safety-007.kernbefund: The study compared crash data at 18 DOOH sites with control points downstream on the same routes. Result: significantly elevated crash rates directly at and immediately after digital billboards. The analysis controlled for road geometry and traffic volume. This is one of the most frequently cited real-world crash studies in the Scenic America compendium (the leading US organization opposing highway advertising).
safety-007.relevanz: Digital billboards on high-speed roads demonstrably increase the risk of accidents for all road users. The societal costs — medical treatment, property damage, productivity losses — are externalized onto the general public, while the profit remains with the OOH (out-of-home advertising) operator. Road authorities that grant DOOH concessions on high-speed roads thereby transfer a documented safety risk to the public.

urban-001.zusammenfassung: An empirical comparative study (UK and Brazil) on the negative effects of commercial signage and advertising on the visual quality of urban spaces and the quality of life of residents. Examined from architectural, planning, and psychological perspectives.
urban-001.kernbefund: Commercial signage and outdoor advertising have demonstrably negative consequences for the visual quality of urban spaces and the well-being of residents. The study establishes that visual overload from advertising acts as an environmental stressor.
urban-001.relevanz: The book is one of the most comprehensive scientific analyses of outdoor advertising as a source of visual pollution. It shows that advertising in public space destroys the character of cities and measurably reduces quality of life — irrespective of whether residents consciously perceive advertising or not.

urban-002.zusammenfassung: Development of a methodology for measuring visual pollution caused by outdoor advertising on urban streets, combining intervisibility analysis with public surveys. Demonstrates that over-stimulating advertising is a quantifiable source of visual pollution.
urban-002.kernbefund: Outdoor advertising is a measurable source of visual pollution on urban streets. Cities lack standardized measurement methods, which makes effective regulation impossible. The study provides, for the first time, a scientific tool for quantifying the problem.
urban-002.relevanz: The absence of measurement methods and standards allows the advertising industry to visually burden public space without limit, while cities are unable to effectively constrain this. The study shows that the problem is real, measurable, and amenable to regulation.

urban-003.zusammenfassung: A European comparative study on urban visual pollution, published in Nature Scientific Reports. Shows that visual pollution is far more than an aesthetic problem — it acts as an environmental stressor with direct health consequences.
urban-003.kernbefund: Visual pollution is a significant environmental problem driven by rapid urbanization. It is not merely an aesthetic nuisance, but acts directly on mental health: it contributes to anxiety, stress, and reduced quality of life. Advertising is one of the primary drivers of visual pollution in urban spaces.
urban-003.relevanz: In cities with high advertising density, residents demonstrably suffer from higher stress levels. Outdoor advertising is a primary, avoidable contributor to this burden.

urban-004.zusammenfassung: A critical urban analysis of outdoor advertising as a mechanism for privatizing public space. Examines how advertising imposes a specific "order" on the cityscape and undermines democratic control over public space.
urban-004.kernbefund: Advertising imposes a particular "spatial order" (Raumordnung) on public space that places commercial interests above public interests. Regulatory mechanisms operating under the label of "public accountability" serve commercial interests in practice. The "advertising city" dispossesses citizens of their shared urban space (urban commons).
urban-004.relevanz: Public space belongs to everyone — advertising turns it into an instrument of private profit interests. Citizens have no choice as to whether their fields of vision and attention are used for commercial purposes.

urban-005.zusammenfassung: A systematic literature review on visual pollution as an environmental problem. Identifies research gaps and methodological approaches to measurement and regulation. Published in 2024 in MDPI Land.
urban-005.kernbefund: Visual pollution is a recognized and growing environmental problem. Research shows consistent negative impacts on well-being and urban quality. Outdoor advertising is one of the primary drivers, yet it is barely captured by urban environmental regulations.
urban-005.relevanz: The study explicitly identifies outdoor advertising as a primary source of visual pollution and demonstrates that existing regulatory instruments are insufficient. It provides a comprehensive scientific framework for policy measures.

urban-006.zusammenfassung: The hardware design of so-called "double posters" (City-Light-Boards — freestanding double-sided advertising panels, typically found at transit stops) has far-reaching consequences for the architecture of public space, as they physically intrude into pavements and pedestrian zones.
urban-006.kernbefund: While traditional posters are usually mounted flat against walls, double-sided advertising installations (often 2 to 3 metres tall) are installed freestanding and perpendicular to the direction of pedestrian flow in order to guarantee maximum visibility from both directions. Studies show that this placement narrows pavements, restricts accessibility for wheelchair users, and cuts through urban sightlines.
urban-006.relevanz: The hardware of double-poster units privatizes actual physical space (the pavement) and subordinates pedestrians' freedom of movement to the visibility of advertising messages.

urban-007.zusammenfassung: Visual pollution from outdoor advertising does not merely harm aesthetics, but has directly measurable negative economic impacts on residents.
urban-007.kernbefund: Analyses of the US real estate market show that close proximity to commercial billboards (so-called "billboard blight") significantly reduces the value of adjacent residential properties. The contributing factors include light pollution from illumination or digital LEDs, the destruction of sightlines, and the psychological association of billboards with neglect and pure commercialization. This is particularly problematic because billboards have historically been concentrated disproportionately in already low-income neighborhoods (a pattern linked to "redlining" — the discriminatory practice of denying services to residents in minority neighborhoods).
urban-007.relevanz: Outdoor advertising redistributes wealth: advertising conglomerates generate profits while residents bear the real costs through noise, light, and declining property values (negative externalities).

urban-009.zusammenfassung: Digital Out-of-Home (DOOH) installations violate the boundaries of private space by emitting unsolicited light into homes and bedrooms.
urban-009.kernbefund: In urban planning, the phenomenon of "light trespass" (Lichteinbruch — the unwanted intrusion of light into private spaces) is regarded as a form of spatial boundary violation. DOOH screens often emit light in an undirected manner, illuminating the facades and interiors of nearby residents as if it were daylight. Because the light is commercial and often dynamic (changing images, flashing), it is psychologically harder to ignore than static street lighting. Affected residents report a massive reduction in quality of life and the feeling that, even within their own four walls, they can no longer escape the pressure of advertising.
urban-009.relevanz: Advertising conglomerates privatize citizens' attention by visually occupying their private spaces. The right to darkness and retreat in one's own home is subordinated to commercial interests.

health-014.zusammenfassung: In July 2023, the WHO published its first normative guidance on food marketing to children. For the first time, the WHO explicitly recommends mandatory statutory measures — not voluntary self-regulation — and expressly includes outdoor advertising in public spaces as a regulatory target.
health-014.kernbefund: The WHO finds that industry self-regulation has failed and that "effective mandatory measures by member states" are required. The guideline covers all marketing channels including OOH advertising and calls for clear nutrient profiling to define HFSS products (high in fat, sugar, salt) that must not be marketed to children.
health-014.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is explicitly within the scope of the WHO guideline. Since children are inevitably exposed to billboards, DOOH screens, and posters, the WHO requirements apply directly to the OOH industry. Many EU countries are using this guideline as the basis for national legislation.

health-015.zusammenfassung: Since 1 January 2026, the United Kingdom has enforced a complete advertising ban on HFSS products (High in Fat, Sugar, Salt) in outdoor advertising. The ban covers all paid-for OOH media — digital screens, traditional posters, and transit advertising. It is the first nationally enforced HFSS ban for the outdoor advertising sector worldwide.
health-015.kernbefund: The UK ban covers all forms of out-of-home advertising and applies to products classified as unhealthy under the Government Nutrient Profile Model. Fast food chains, confectionery manufacturers, and soft drink brands are directly affected. Violations are sanctioned by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA).
health-015.relevanz: The UK regulation demonstrates that democratically mandated governments can and will enforce comprehensive OOH advertising bans for health-harmful products. Since HFSS products are among the most profitable booking categories for the DOOH industry, the UK model directly threatens the business models of international OOH conglomerates.

health-016.zusammenfassung: Lithuania banned all alcohol advertising — including outdoor advertising and OOH — in 2018. A longitudinal study published in the BMJ in 2025 with 84,189 participants causally documents that the advertising ban has significantly reduced alcohol consumption and alcohol-related diseases. It is one of the methodologically strongest pieces of evidence for the causal effect of advertising bans on consumer behaviour.
health-016.kernbefund: The study uses a natural experiment: before/after the ban in Lithuania vs. a control group in Latvia (without a ban). The authors find statistically significant reductions in alcohol consumption, binge drinking, and alcohol-related mortality. The study design allows causal conclusions, not merely correlations.
health-016.relevanz: Alcohol OOH advertising is legal and widespread in many EU countries. The Lithuania study is the strongest causal evidence to date that a national OOH advertising ban for health-harmful products measurably saves lives. It is already being used by health authorities in Germany and Austria as a reference for national legislative initiatives.

health-017.zusammenfassung: The Children's Food Advertising Act (KLWG-E) introduced in Germany in 2024 was intended to restrict advertising for unhealthy foods targeting children under 14 — originally including outdoor advertising. Following intensive lobbying by the food industry and the advertising sector, the OOH domain was largely excluded from the scope of the law.
health-017.kernbefund: foodwatch and other consumer protection organisations documented that the draft was weakened in more than 40 points through lobbying interventions. The OOH sector was not regulated as an independent medium. The remaining restrictions apply primarily to TV and online — billboards and DOOH screens in front of schools, playgrounds, and daycare centres remain largely uncontrolled.
health-017.relevanz: Germany had the opportunity, as the largest EU market, to set a precedent for OOH child-marketing bans. The failure of OOH regulation reveals the lobbying weight of the outdoor advertising industry in German politics. It simultaneously demonstrates that legislative gaps in the OOH sector do not arise by chance, but are actively produced.

reg-027.zusammenfassung: In May 2024, the City of Edinburgh Council resolved to no longer permit advertising for fossil fuels and arms products on all municipal advertising spaces. Edinburgh thereby became the first city to explicitly ban both categories simultaneously from public advertising space.
reg-027.kernbefund: The Edinburgh ban applies to all municipal advertising contracts and council-owned spaces. The city references its climate commitments and the Edinburgh Climate Pledge. The ban covers airlines, oil companies, and arms manufacturers, and affects contracts with JCDecaux and Clear Channel, which operate municipal advertising spaces in Edinburgh.
reg-027.relevanz: The combination of fossil fuel and military advertising bans sets a new European standard. Edinburgh demonstrates that municipalities can directly regulate the outdoor advertising industry through the contractual design of their own concessions — without having to wait for national legislation.

reg-028.zusammenfassung: In 2023, the Stockholm Region resolved to no longer permit advertising for fossil products and gambling on all regional advertising spaces (metro, buses, government buildings). In 2024, the Swedish Administrative Court confirmed the legality of the ban following a lawsuit brought by the outdoor advertising industry.
reg-028.kernbefund: The Administrative Court ruled that public bodies have the right to define categories of advertising incompatible with their ethical and ecological commitments. The ruling creates precedent for Scandinavian municipalities. All advertising contracts of the Stockholm Region are affected.
reg-028.relevanz: The Stockholm ruling strengthens the right of municipal and regional authorities across Europe to ban advertising categories on their own spaces. Since public transport advertising is one of the most lucrative OOH segments, the ruling represents a direct economic threat to Clear Channel and JCDecaux, which hold Stockholm contracts.

reg-029.zusammenfassung: Genoa resolved in 2025 and Florence in 2026 to ban advertising for fossil fuels and high-emission products (long-haul flights, internal combustion engines) on municipal advertising spaces. Both cities are pioneers in Southern Europe and are setting a trend for other Italian municipalities.
reg-029.kernbefund: The bans follow the model of Amsterdam, The Hague, and Edinburgh and extend to direct advertising for fossil energy providers, short-haul flights, cruises, and new cars with internal combustion engines. Florence explicitly justifies the ban on the grounds of protecting the UNESCO World Heritage cityscape from commercial overload, as well as climate targets.
reg-029.relevanz: The spread of fossil fuel advertising bans to Southern Europe shows that the model is not a Northern European niche. With Florence and Genoa, strategically significant precedents are being established for further Mediterranean metropolises. The loss of these booking volumes directly affects the OOH industry.

reg-030.zusammenfassung: In December 2024, the UK Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) banned an outdoor advertising campaign by Lloyds Bank that positioned itself as climate-friendly, even though the bank is one of the largest financiers of fossil fuels in Great Britain. This is one of the first cases in which a financial institution has been explicitly condemned for greenwashing in OOH media.
reg-030.kernbefund: The ASA found that the advertisements created a misleading impression of Lloyds' climate efforts. The bank had placed outdoor screens with CO2-neutrality messaging while its lending portfolio, according to analysis by the NGO ShareAction, has billions invested in oil and gas companies. The ASA ruling ordered the immediate withdrawal of all OOH materials.
reg-030.relevanz: Greenwashing in OOH campaigns is increasingly being penalised by independent regulators. This ruling shows that industries outside the direct fossil fuel sector can also be confronted with outdoor advertising bans when their advertising message contradicts their actual environmental impact.

reg-031.zusammenfassung: With the entry into force of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act, the UK competition authority CMA received from April 2025 the power to impose direct fines of up to 10% of global annual turnover on companies making misleading environmental claims in advertising campaigns — including OOH advertising. Previously, the CMA could only bring court proceedings.
reg-031.kernbefund: The CMA's Green Claims Code prohibits vague statements such as "sustainable", "eco-friendly", or "carbon-neutral" without scientifically verifiable evidence. The new enforcement powers allow direct sanctions without litigation. For large OOH operators and their advertising clients, this means that any greenwashing campaign can now directly lead to billion-pound fines.
reg-031.relevanz: OOH spaces are a preferred medium for greenwashing campaigns — large-format images with green imagery and sustainability promises. The CMA powers affect both advertisers (turnover penalty) and potentially OOH network operators if they participate in the dissemination of misleading content.

reg-032.zusammenfassung: The Hague was the first city in the world to ban OOH advertising for fossil fuels, internal-combustion-engine new cars, cruise ships, and fossil-fuel airlines, effective 2024. The outdoor advertising industry filed a legal challenge. In April 2025, the District Court of The Hague dismissed the lawsuit in its entirety and confirmed the legality of the ban.
reg-032.kernbefund: The court ruled that municipalities may legitimately determine, within the scope of their property rights and climate protection obligations, which categories of advertising are no longer acceptable on municipal surfaces. The ruling explicitly confirms applicability to all forms of OOH media, including DOOH. It is considered a precedent-setting judgment for the entire EU.
reg-032.relevanz: The ruling closes the last legal loophole: advertising conglomerates can no longer block municipal fossil-fuel bans through litigation. This substantially accelerates the domino effect of bans across Europe. All OOH operators holding municipal contracts in the EU must now assume that similar lawsuits will fail.

reg-033.zusammenfassung: In October 2024, the Spanish competition authority CNMC prohibited the planned acquisition of Clear Channel's Spanish operations by JCDecaux. The regulators found that the merger would create a dominant market position that permanently eliminates competition in the Spanish OOH market.
reg-033.kernbefund: The CNMC analysis concluded that following a successful acquisition JCDecaux would control over 70% of premium OOH surfaces in major Spanish cities. The authority found no adequate remedies to compensate for the competitive distortions. The proceedings demonstrate that EU competition authorities are actively combating structural market concentration in the OOH sector.
reg-033.relevanz: The decision confirms what the EU Commission had already established in earlier cases (JCDecaux Brussels, reg-023): the OOH sector is prone to oligopolistic structures that require state intervention. Cities and municipalities that enter into contracts with OOH corporations do so within a structurally imbalanced power dynamic.

reg-034.zusammenfassung: UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in the Climate Context, Ian Fry, called in a June 2025 report to the UN Human Rights Council for criminal prosecution of companies and advertising agencies that disseminate misleading fossil-fuel advertising. He classifies greenwashing outdoor advertising as a violation of the human right to a safe, clean, healthy, and sustainable environment.
reg-034.kernbefund: Fry argues that companies that continue to place deceptive advertising despite knowledge of the climate harms of fossil fuels expose themselves to criminal liability. He recommends that UN member states enact national legislation defining greenwashing as a criminal offence and including OOH advertising operators that distribute such content.
reg-034.relevanz: The classification of greenwashing OOH advertising as a human rights violation by a UN mandate holder represents a paradigm shift. OOH network operators broadcasting campaigns for fossil fuel corporations are for the first time positioned as potential co-responsible parties in international human rights discourse. Pressure on institutional investors in JCDecaux, Clear Channel, and Ströer is likely to increase.

psych-010.zusammenfassung: A meta-analysis of 95 experimental studies published in Frontiers in Psychology (2025) concludes that advertising featuring idealised body images causally produces body dissatisfaction, self-esteem problems, and disordered eating behaviour in adolescents and young adults. It is the most comprehensive synthesis of causal evidence on this topic to date.
psych-010.kernbefund: The meta-analysis finds significant, consistent effects across 95 experiments: exposure to idealised body images in advertising increases body dissatisfaction (effect size d=0.58), depressive mood (d=0.41), and disordered eating behaviour (d=0.37). The effects hold across all genders and are particularly strong in early teenagers.
psych-010.relevanz: Outdoor advertising is the most public of all advertising channels — children and adolescents cannot avoid it. The systematic evidence of this meta-analysis directly supports legislative bans on idealising body images in OOH campaigns. The psychological harm caused by outdoor advertising is therefore no longer scientifically deniable.

pol-016.zusammenfassung: Ströer SE & Co. KGaA reported record revenues of over €2 billion for the 2024 financial year and states it controls approximately 80% of DOOH advertising surfaces in Germany. The company markets more than 500,000 advertising structures in public space — giving a single corporation monopoly control over the visual landscape of German city centres.
pol-016.kernbefund: Market concentration at Ströer has grown continuously since 2010. Ströer holds exclusive concession contracts with cities, municipalities, and Deutsche Bahn with terms of 10–25 years. At the same time, the corporation is investing heavily in DOOH conversions that inherit existing permits without new approval procedures. The €2B revenue figure is more than double the total public-sector expenditure on urban green space in Germany.
pol-016.relevanz: When a single publicly listed company controls 80% of the national DOOH market while using public space under conditions that bind cities for decades, a structural dependency arises that makes democratic regulation more difficult. Ströer's lobbying power is proportional to its market power.

priv-005.zusammenfassung: The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), in force since August 2024, classifies biometric categorisation systems in public space as high-risk. Systems that infer emotion, age, gender, or ethnicity from camera footage are subject to strict requirements or are prohibited. DOOH audience measurement technology (Anonymized Video Analytics) falls directly within this regulatory scope.
priv-005.kernbefund: Article 5 of the AI Act prohibits, with effect from February 2025, the real-time analysis of biometric characteristics for the purpose of categorising persons in publicly accessible spaces without explicit authorisation. Most DOOH audience measurement systems (JCDecaux Smart, Clear Channel Live, Ströer Data Analytics) use precisely these technologies. The Commerzbank cooperation with Ströer for target-group analysis would no longer be legal under Art. 5 of the AI Act.
priv-005.relevanz: DOOH screens equipped with cameras for audience analysis become a heavily regulated high-risk area under the EU AI Act. The data collection promise that enables programmatic DOOH targeting is highly legally uncertain under EU law. Advertisers relying on audience data from DOOH network operators expose themselves to liability risks.

safety-008.title_en: EU Commission: Roadside Advertising Identified as a Significant Source of Driver Distraction (2023)
safety-008.zusammenfassung: A thematic report by the European Commission on road safety classifies roadside advertising as a relevant external source of driver distraction.
safety-008.kernbefund: The report establishes that visual stimuli outside the vehicle, particularly (digital) billboards, can significantly distract drivers' attention from the driving task. The increasing complexity and dynamics of Digital Out-of-Home (DOOH) displays amplify this effect, as they are designed to actively capture the gaze. Studies show that drivers exhibit longer glances away from the road when near such installations, which measurably increases the risk of accidents. The EU Commission therefore recommends stricter regulation of the location and design of roadside advertising.
safety-008.relevanz: While the industry often claims its installations are safe, this official EU report confirms that the commercial exploitation of drivers' field of vision represents a systematic safety risk in road traffic.

res-012.title_en: DarkSky International: Electronic Billboards are up to Ten Times Brighter than Traditional Billboards
res-012.zusammenfassung: The organization DarkSky International documents that electronic billboards (LED) have massively higher light emissions than illuminated static posters, leading to significant light pollution.
res-012.kernbefund: Digital billboards often emit light directly into the environment instead of illuminating a surface. Measurements show that at night they can be up to ten times brighter than traditional billboards illuminated from above. This extreme brightness contributes massively to 'skyglow,' disrupts the orientation of nocturnal animals (insects, birds), and affects the circadian rhythm of residents. DarkSky recommends strict limits for luminance (candelas per m²) and automatic shutdown systems during night hours.
res-012.relevanz: The switch from paper to digital is often marketed as 'more efficient,' but ignores the massive ecological costs of light pollution, which do not exist to this extent with conventional posters.

priv-006.title_en: Big Brother Watch: DOOH Screens Secretly Use Biometric Facial Detection for Audience Analysis
priv-006.zusammenfassung: The civil rights organization Big Brother Watch warns of the massive use of surveillance technology in digital advertising columns that capture biometric data from passers-by without their consent.
priv-006.kernbefund: Cameras integrated into modern DOOH installations use 'face detection' software to analyze the age, gender, ethnicity, and emotional response of passers-by in real-time. Although providers claim the data is anonymized, the collection of biometric characteristics takes place in public space without citizens being able to evade or object. Big Brother Watch classifies this as a structural violation of privacy and a step towards comprehensive biometric surveillance of society.
priv-006.relevanz: Public space is transformed into a commercial surveillance laboratory by this technology. Passers-by are degraded into data sources for the advertising industry without being asked.

psych-011.title_en: University of Warwick: Advertising Expenditure Correlates Negatively with Life Satisfaction in 27 European Countries
psych-011.zusammenfassung: A large-scale study by the University of Warwick shows a significant correlation between high advertising expenditure and declining life satisfaction in the population.
psych-011.kernbefund: An analysis of data from 27 European countries over several decades proves that an increase in advertising investment correlates with a subsequent decline in average well-being. Researchers attribute this to the creation of artificial needs and the constant social comparison (status anxiety) fueled by advertising. Outdoor advertising plays a special role here, as it is unavoidable in public space and thus exerts permanent psychological pressure on all social strata.
psych-011.relevanz: The ubiquitous visual presence of unattainable lifestyles in the city acts as a systematic disruptive factor for the mental health of urban society.

equity-005.title_en: Adfree Cities Mapping: Disproportionate Concentration of Outdoor Advertising in Socially Disadvantaged Neighborhoods (2023)
equity-005.zusammenfassung: A mapping study by Adfree Cities proves that billboards are systematically placed more frequently in poorer urban neighborhoods, while wealthier areas remain largely ad-free.
equity-005.kernbefund: Spatial analysis shows a correlation between the deprivation index of a neighborhood and the density of outdoor advertising installations. Residents in socially disadvantaged areas are exposed to a significantly higher 'visual load' from advertising, especially for harmful products such as fast food, gambling, and alcohol. This reinforces existing health and social inequalities, as the affected population groups can hardly avoid the commercial pressure in their immediate living environment.
equity-005.relevanz: The distribution of advertising space is a matter of social justice. Poorer neighborhoods are instrumentalized as 'advertising zones,' while protection from commercial harassment is considered the standard in rich neighborhoods.
